speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT OF AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce the appointment of Robert James Rankin, vice-chairman of the national harbours board, to the office of president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority as of August 1. Mr. Rankin will succeed B. J. Roberts, C.B.E., president of the seaway authority since February, 1958, who retires on July 31. Mr. Rankin has been vice-chairman of the national harbours board since February 1, 1958.
In going to his new post Mr. Rankin will add to his already extensive experience in marine matters. He formerly served as chairman of the port of Halifax commission for five years, and was a member of the commission at the time of his appointment as vice-chairman of the national harbours board. He played a notable role prior to that appointment in the economic development of the Atlantic provinces, and was president of the Atlantic provinces economic council in 1957. He is a former newspaperman, joining the staff of the Halifax Herald in 1921 and rising to the post of managing editor of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald before being named vice-president and member of the board of directors. He is a past president of the Canadian Press, serving in that capacity from 1954 to 1956.
Mr. Rankin was born in Chatham, Ontario, a son of the late Mr. and Mrs. J. B. Rankin, and received his education in the schools there. His wife is the former Constance Marguerite Buckler of Annapolis Royal. They have two sons. Mr. Rankin is a veteran of world war I, serving as signals officer with the 1st battalion, C.E.F.
I would also like to refer to the notable contribution Mr. B. J. Roberts has made to Canada over a long period of years. He is a former member and chairman of the national harbours board and a former assistant 79951-0-3124
deputy minister of finance. Over a period of 30 years he served on a number of important boards and commissions, and he was financial adviser to the British commonwealth air training plan during world war II. He was named a commander of the British empire after the war ended.
Mr. Roberts took over as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority early in 1958, and supervised the final year of construction and the operation of the project since its opening in April last year. His contribution to the present successful operation of the seaway has been a very real one indeed.

1.	Has the government received a copy of the 1959 report of the international commission on radiological protection?
2.	If so, has the government taken any steps to follow the recommendations of this report insofar as lowering the permissible strontium 90 level in food and water is concerned?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to part 1 is yes.
The answer to part 2 is as follows. The data contained in the new report of the international commission on radiological protection have been used in the preparation of the annual report of the radiation protection division for 1959. They will continue to form a basis for interpretation of the findings of my department until further recommendations are published by the international commission on radiological protection.
It is to be emphasized, however, that the recommended maximum permissible concentrations given in the new report do not refer to food, but only to air and water. Using additional data contained in the report, members of my department have calculated a maximum permissible level of strontium 90 in the average diet of Canadians. This figure is 79 micromicrocuries strontium 90 per gram of calcium as compared with the ICRP value for water of 33 micromicrocuries strontium 90 per litre. The previous permissible level for strontium 90 in the average Canadian diet based on the 1955 ICRP recommendations was similarly calculated to be 98 micromicrocuries per gram of calcium.

subtopic: SARNIA, ONT.    STATEMENT ON REPORTED THREAT TO DISPOSSESS KENNETH PLAIN

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of
Citizenship and Immigration): Mr. Speaker, on Monday the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) inquired concerning the reported eviction of Mr. Kenneth Plain, a member of the Sarnia band, from property held by him on the Sarnia Indian reserve.
Mr. Plain held two parcels of land that were surrendered by the band and sold on terms set by the band in the surrender itself. One parcel comprised 2 acres, the other 9.6 acres. For his interest in these two parcels together Mr. Plain agreed to accept $36,000. The 2 acre parcel has already been paid for in full and title transferred. Mr. Plain received $6,206.90. Total payments made to him amount to $12,612.49. While his valuation of his house located on the 2 acre parcel appears to have been included in the over-all price, he has the right to remove it within six months from the date the purchase price has been paid in full.
Mr. Plain apparently contends that he is not required to move his house until payment has been made in full for both parcels of land. They do not adjoin one another.
The matter has been studied from a legal and equitable standpoint, and it would appear that from neither angle is Mr. Plain on sound ground. Legally the conditions of sale are governed by the surrender itself and the sale contract, not by the option signed by him, which is invalid under section 28 of the Indian Act. The importance of the option is its evidence of his agreement as to price.
Equitably he has already received a substantial payment on account of his house, which was valued in 1957 at $7,000, and may 
move it. The balance owing on the 9.6 acre parcel will be paid to him when the sale of it is completed. If the sale should fall through his ownership of the parcel will be re-established, and he will retain what had been paid thereon.
The purchaser has given Mr. Plain more than the six months' notice required to move his house, and desires possession in order that the land may be used as intended. I may say that the matter is really outside the control of my department, as title has passed.

speechtext: Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Essex East asked about the disarmament conference, and today there may be further questions arising from the tabling by the Prime Minister yesterday of the exchange of letters between himself and Mr. Khrushchev about the latest Soviet disarmament proposals. Perhaps I could deal with this situation by making a brief statement on the Canadian position at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the minister leave to make a statement at this time?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In the Canadian view it is important that in these negotiations all ten nations represented on the committee should lose no opportunity to explore every possible avenue of progress in disarmament. The Canadian delegation has constantly in mind, and tries to make certain that the whole committee bears in mind, that not only two nations or ten nations but all the nations of the world have a vital interest in disarmament. It is certain that the members of the committee will be held to account by the other nations of the world if they neglect opportunities for progress in disarmament.
It was in this spirit that the Prime Minister replied to Mr. Khrushchev's letter forwarding the latest Soviet proposals. The Canadian government wants these proposals to receive a patient and searching examination in the ten-nation committee, as marking the opening of a phase of detailed, businesslike and uninterrupted negotiations. We believed that there should be no hasty, ill-considered reaction to the new Soviet proposals, but the most careful and constructive examination of these proposals in the committee which circumstances permit. General Burns has been instructed accordingly, and I am happy to say that the other members of the western five on the committee fully shared this view.

I am particularly glad to report this unanimous view of the western representatives because, as the house is aware, the members of the western group have had their differences from time to time in the past. The Canadian delegation for its part has, on several occasions, been instructed to present views contrary to those expressed by other members of the western five, whenever this seemed warranted. We would not hesitate to authorize the Canadian delegation to follow a similarly independent line again if circumstances so dictated. But for the present no such need exists, and M. Moch has rightly stressed the solidarity of the western five in the statement to which the hon. member for Essex East referred. The western five advanced their proposals some time ago and indicated their willingness to enter upon detailed negotiations. The eastern nations are now speaking in support of the new Soviet proposals of June 2, and have indicated that these provide a basis for negotiation. These latest proposals are now being further explained by the eastern countries, partly as a result of questioning by the western members of the committee.
In the course of this clarification on June 9 General Burns pointed to several examples of ways in which the new Soviet proposals represent an advance over earlier Soviet positions; for instance, with respect to the prohibition of weapons of mass destruction in outer space; the control over launching of rockets for peaceful purposes; the provision for a joint study of the cessation of production of nuclear weapons and destruction of stockpiles; and the inclusion of measures for peacekeeping machinery in accordance with the United Nations charter. In making this statement, General Bums emphasized that the Canadian delegation wished to approach the new Soviet proposals in the most constructive way. He chose the examples I have mentioned because they are among the measures to which the Canadian government attaches special significance.
It is my view that the time has come, perhaps through an examination of equivalent features of new Soviet proposals and the western proposals, to begin a process of negotiation of balanced concessions. This was the sort of package approach to which I referred earlier in the house when I reported on the NATO ministerial meeting at Istanbul. I should like to emphasize, however, that by "package" I do not mean that the one side or the other should hold out for its present proposals on an all or nothing basis; the packages I have in mind, as I have tried to explain, are smaller and would contain provisions of equivalent significance to both sides. The goal would remain general and complete

Inquiries of the Ministry disarmament under effective international control, but it would be accomplished by a stage by stage process throughout which concessions would be balanced in such a way that neither side would obtain a temporary military superiority.
For the first time in these negotiations the Soviet delegation has admitted that there will have to be some sort of international machinery to maintain peace in a disarmed world. The proposals are also considerably more detailed and therefore less obscure than the proposals Mr. Khrushchev made to the general assembly of the United Nations in 1959. They also make some provision for the initiation of a process of study before measures of disarmament are actually taken. This is important because no responsible government will agree to any disarmament proposal, much less a complex of disarmament measures, until it has reached a clear understanding with the other governments concerned of the exact implications of agreement.
Therefore I believe that attention should now be given to the possibility of negotiating on parts, if not on the whole, of the two plans. In the course of the next few days in Geneva General Burns will be making suggestions as to how this necessary process might be undertaken through joint studies.

Mr. Speaker, the house will welcome this statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, which in a general way brings us up to date in regard to the current discussions in the ten power disarmament committee. I must say, however, that we are not really further advanced in our appreciation of the possibilities of progress.
It will be remembered that when this matter was first discussed during the present session the minister expressed a strong note of optimism indicating that he believed that we would see progress in the field of disarmament. Unfortunately events have not borne out the minister's assurances and anticipations. The minister now tempers his optimism by the realities of the situation.
The last proposal of Chairman Khrushchev does not seem to represent anything fundamentally new or different from proposals already made, and seems to bear many resemblances to the proposal put forward by Mr. Jules Moch, the delegate of France, a short time ago, particularly the implementation of a partial disarmament program directed toward eliminating the means of delivering nuclear weapons to targets.
What I believe this parliament had hoped to receive from the minister, and what I believe this country expects to receive from

the minister, is some indication of the government's determination to display the kind of independence about which the minister spoke when he participated in the foreign affairs debate in February in this house. As the minister said, Canada is a member of the ten power group. In some respects she holds the position of representing not only the viewpoint of Canadians but of the middle powers and the smaller nations of the world.
We have not yet had, it seems, any indication of the determination of this government and of its spokesmen to take independent positions where these can properly and constructively be taken. The minister referred to one of the initiatives that seemed to establish that the Canadian government had taken an independent position, but he did not give any indication of what that independent position was.

Mr. Chairman, there is nothing controversial in the bill. It was before the committee on veterans affairs, was carefully studied by that committee and has been recommended to this committee without amendment.
The purpose of this bill was explained when the resolution was before us a few days ago. Hon. members will recall that there are two main provisions. The first provides for the payment of the war veterans allowance to recipients outside of Canada. The second provision is designed to establish a corresponding Canadian residence qualification for former members of our armed forces or those of our allies who served during world war II, thus allowing treatment of these veterans on a basis similar to that now available to veterans of our armed forces or those of our allies who served in earlier wars. There is nothing further I need say at the present time, but I would be pleased to answer any questions hon. members have.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ABSENTEE PAYMENTS, RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I was not able to attend the sittings of the veterans committee when this bill was under discussion. For the purpose of clarification I should like to ask one or two questions which I think could be properly asked on this first clause.

As I understand the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act there are three separate groups of veterans who can qualify for these benefits. The first group comprises veterans who are 60 years of age and over who can qualify without a means test. The second group comprises veterans under 60 who can qualify if they are totally and permanently unemployable. The third group comprises veterans who are in receipt of a pension, but whose pension is less than the ceiling permitted under the veterans charter and therefore they are eligible to receive a supplementary payment through the war veterans allowance to bring their total income up to the ceiling.
I gather that all three groups are qualified to benefit under this bill provided they are in receipt of the allowance before they leave Canada and have resided here for 12 months piror to leaving, with the exception of the imperial veterans, of course, who have to be in Canada for 10 years to qualify.
Since the means test applies to these veterans, are they permitted to draw the war veterans allowance for a full 12 months while outside Canada? If so, what machinery exists in case their income changes during their absence? That would affect the means test under which they receive it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ABSENTEE PAYMENTS, RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo is quite correct in saying there are three types of war veterans allowance recipients. All are subject to the means test, even the veteran who is a pensioner. As far as the 12 months' residence period is concerned, those affected will be entitled to receive the war veterans allowance outside of Canada but they will be subject to a means test just the same. If they are living in Great Britain our offices there will see that a means test of some kind is applied. I refer to those who will leave Canada and go to Great Britain. Those in the United States who are properly qualified recipients when they leave Canada will also be subject to review by some official in our consular offices in the United States, or whatever country in which they may be living.

I agree that it does represent some new and probably unusual problems. In fact that was the reason given by the former minister for refusing to introduce legislation

I do suggest to the minister that it might be advisable for the department to publish a small pamphlet dealing with this act, to explain in simple language to persons who might apply just what the amendments mean. Although the bill is relatively simple to hon. members who have had some experience in reading legislation, and even though it might be quite clear to one who has dealt with legislation, it would not be clear to some people. I suggest it would be advisable to have a small pamphlet printed pointing out the terms of the legislation and informing the veterans or the dependants seeking information how to proceed to make application and what would happen with respect to their payments and so on when they went overseas. I make that suggestion. It could be done in a two-page pamphlet, and it would be of great assistance. The number that would be required would be relatively small indeed.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two in reply to the statement made by the Postmaster General when he replied to the hon. member for St. John's East on June 8. The hon. member for St. John's East had asked the Postmaster General to reconsider the present policy of not providing post office buildings for small revenue offices, and he went on to outline conditions in his own riding.
Earlier I had made a similar plea to the minister, as recorded at page 4298 of Hansard of May 27. In the course of my remarks on that day I suggested to the minister that the post office buildings were classified on the basis of revenue, because a post office building is not supplied unless the revenue exceeds $3,000. When the minister replied to me the same day he said, as recorded on page 4305 of Hansard:
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo spoke a little while ago, and I would tell him that the classification of post offices does not rest on revenue but rests on a unit of work basis.
The reply made by the minister to the hon. member for St. John's East on June 8 does not conform with the statement the minister made in replying to me. As found on page 4705 of Hansard the Postmaster General made the following reply to the hon. member for St. John's East:
As to the hon. member for St. John's East who spoke about revenue post offices in Newfoundland, may I say that we can have but one policy for buildings right across Canada. I think the weakness in the suggestion he put forward-and I say this without any criticism-was contained in his own observation that in these areas where they would like to have a government building constructed they cannot afford one for themselves and the postmaster cannot afford to put a special one up because his revenue is only a few hundred dollars a year.
That was the very point I was trying to make. I do not want to take the time to elaborate on it, because I have already spoken about the matter on previous occasions. However, I think the Postmaster General's own argument is weak when he says that the policy is based on the revenue and that because these little post offices only generate

revenue of a few hundred dollars they do not deserve any special consideration with respect to accommodation.
I wish to point out to the Postmaster General that the spending of 5 cents for a stamp in one of these small post offices, which has a total revenue of only $400 or $500 a year, generates probably $2 or $3 in revenue in some other post office in Canada. I know that most of the post offices in my riding are small revenue operations and come within this classification, but the revenue of the Moncton post office and of the St. John's post office is greatly increased because of the revenue generated in these small offices. A person sends a letter with a 5 cent stamp on it to a mail order house such as Eaton's or Simpson's in Moncton, Halifax or St. John's, and as a result the revenue in the other post office will be many times the 5 cent stamp. It may be a couple of dollars.
I think the minister's argument is weak on that score, because it is the total revenue of the post office and the need of the community that should be taken into account. I think these should be the overriding factors. I do not think it is fair to exclude small offices on the basis of revenue. I pointed out to the Postmaster General the other day that this results in discrimination between one postmaster and another. In his reply to the hon. member for St. John's East the other day the minister went on to say:
In these circumstances there is very little point in putting up a special government building. We depend upon local quarters provided by the postmaster.
In my opinion such a policy is discriminatory as between one postmaster in one settlement and another postmaster in another settlement. An undue burden is placed on the postmaster when he has to find accommodation, and there is discrimination between settlements where such accommodation is readily available and other settlements of smaller size and smaller revenue where suitable accommodation is not available under any circumstances. I would ask the Postmaster General to take another look at the whole policy and see if something better than what we have at present cannot be worked out.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to lend my support to the query initiated by the hon. member for Port Arthur and supported by other members who have spoken as to the necessity for the use of the words "personal and confidential" on letters we get from the minister. I suppose I could read one letter I have here which is marked "personal and confidential" but because it is so marked perhaps it would not be wise for me to do so. Instead I will

paraphrase it to indicate its contents, and in doing so I do not think I will be violating any confidence.
The letter contains two paragraphs comprising six lines in all. In the first paragraph I am requested to refer to a letter I wrote, and the second paragraph advises me that some information on the matter will be available shortly. That is the gist of the letter. The minister in his replies did not make any specific reference to this point, but as a result of the valid questions asked about the policy of using these words I would have thought that subsequently he might have taken steps to alter his approach to this matter. I find, however, that is not so, because this morning I received another communication from the minister relating to a matter coming under his jurisdiction and it is also marked "personal and confidential".
I realize there are circumstances under which letters might properly be so marked, but to make wholesale use of the words "personal and confidential" on such letters is in my opinion going beyond reasonable limits. I hope the minister will undertake to explain to the house his reasons for the use of the words "personal and confidential". Perhaps he will also undertake to lessen the use of these words on letters in order that members who receive communications from him may, with a clear conscience, communicate to the people responsible for the initiation of the matter in the first place the contents of the minister's letters so they may know what is taking place with respect to the problem of the individual or community, as the case may be.
I should like to deal with some local problems in my constituency, which is primarily a rural one, the largest urban community having a population of 10,000 or 11,000 people. The feeling I wish to convey to the minister applies to other governmental services as well as the postal service. However, so far as postal service is concerned the feeling exists in a number of these rural communities that they tend to suffer because the bulk of postal service and facilities is concentrated in the more heavily settled or urban areas. The people in the smaller communities tend to feel that they are left out of the scheme of things and are not given the consideration they should be given. This feeling relates to the building of post offices, the regularity with which mail is transported in and out of these smaller communities, and a number of other such matters.
Inasmuch as my constituency, as I said, is primarily rural, I should like to make reference to one or two problems there. I hope the minister will undertake to deal with them,
Supply-Post Office
either orally in his answers in the committee but more particularly administratively within his department.
We have one area which has just been opened up by an access road just north of Terrace. I refer to the communities along the Nass river. Prior to a road being built some 75 or 80 miles in length northward to the Nass river, the main contact was by steamer or by their boats down the Nass river to Prince Rupert. However, their main contact is developing with the community of Terrace and along the Nass river. Primarily the people are of Indian origin. There are four Indian villages containing approximately 1,800 people. The Indian affairs branch has recently established in Terrace a new agency which covers these particular Indian communities. That is just another indication that their point of contact with communities other than their own is now through Terrace rather than Prince Rupert, as it was formerly.
The postal service, of course, has not been good in the past although in recent months there have been some changes with regard to the system which existed. There is one community with approximately 400 people namely Greenville. I have been corresponding with the minister about this matter and the people, the band of Indians in that village of Greenville, have also been in communication with the department. I do not know whether they have been in communication with the minister directly but they have been in communication at least with officials of his department. The last time I inquired into this matter, which was a month or so ago, there was what I understand is classified as a winter service which makes a monthly mail delivery from November to April by steamboat or steamer not to the community of Greenville itself but to a community which is a port of call for steamers, called Kincolith.
It is not possible for steamers to operate up the Nass river to Greenville, so they call in at this community of Kincolith further down near the mouth of the Nass river. Then the mail is transferred from Kincolith up to Greenville by boats of individual residents. They follow the fishing industry, and they have quite a number of these boats. They use them to keep in touch with Kincolith and to pick up and deliver their mail. Then, of course, with the mail arriving once a month, many of the people find that unless they can have someone take the mail out for them and mail it at a larger community such as Prince Rupert or Terrace, their correspondence lags back for a period of two months. This is so especially in ordering materials and goods and supplies by mail. They find that they may receive communications on one steamer with

Supply-Post Office
respect to it and be prevented from answering until one month later, when the steamboat calls again at Kincolith.
This matter was raised quite extensively by a letter dated last December 2 from the Greenville council to Mr. Catterall, who I understand is district director of postal services in Vancouver. At least that is the designation given on this letter, and I believe that is the correct title. I wish to read only this one part of it. I might point out that the copy of the letter I have here to Mr. Catterall is dated December 2, 1959 and starts out by saying:
Due to irregular mail schedule I just received your letter of October 29, 1959 a few days ago-
This is a reference to a letter from Mr. Catterall, district director of postal services in Vancouver, which was dated October 29, 1959 and which reached Greenville on the Nass river, as he said "a few days ago", which I would say would be somewhere near the end of November or the first part of December. It therefore took approximately a month from the date of the letter from Mr. Catterall for it to get from the Post Office Department in Vancouver to the people in Greenville.
I relate that incident only to indicate the time that is consumed and the delays involved in letters going into or out of this particular community of Greenville. I make reference only to that community, but others are in the same boat. The correspondence to which I have made reference here and the letter from Mr. Catterall had, in fact, reference to their request for a fortnightly service through Terrace via the road communication or road connection from Terrace up to the Nass river.
From being there and talking to the people I understand there is now postal service by road from Terrace to two other Indian villages on the Nass river, namely Aiyansh and Canyon city. Although the post office is at Aiyansh, there is a fortnightly service from Terrace up the Nass river to Aiyansh. The Greenville people desire-and quite justifiably so, because they are only a few miles down the river from Aiyansh-to be served by postal facilities on the same basis as the communities of Aiyansh and Canyon city. They request a fortnightly service by road from Terrace and back out that way again, because all their communications and their contacts with other communities, as I indicated earlier, are now through and into Terrace rather than the coastal area on down the river to Prince Rupert except during the fishing season, when they fish in and out of that area and use their boats.

As I have said, I have had communications with the minister about this matter, and as far as I can gather from those communications the matter is still under study, in an attempt, I imagine, to get whatever statistical information is necessary as to the volume of mail incoming and outgoing, the regularity with which mail service might be supplied in the future, cost factors and things of that kind. If the minister has some knowledge or information with regard to that matter at this time, it would be helpful if he could indicate it to the committee and to me. However, if it is not immediately available, I will appreciate it greatly if he will tackle this problem with the usual assiduity with which he tackles other problems and will find a solution to it within the shortest possible time.
I also want to make reference, if I may, to another basic problem in the constituency which I represent. This is something about which the minister and I have corresponded, as have many other people, for quite a period of time. It has to do with letter carrier delivery service by postmen in the community of Kitimat.
I wonder if at this stage I might be permitted to make a reference to another matter. This dates back, incidentally, as far as I am personally concerned, to within a few days after I was honoured by being elected in June, 1957, but also goes beyond that to the activities of my predecessor in this house who also dealt with the question. I feel free to make reference to this particular letter from the Postmaster General because this is one which does not have "personal and confidential" marked on it. I might add that it is dated July 15, 1957, so perhaps it predates the institution of the personal and confidential system.
In any event, with respect to establishing postal facilities at Kitimat, the minister was kind enough to write a three-page reply to the query I posed and the request I made to him, and he rejected at that time the possibility of establishing a letter carrier delivery service for five reasons. I will make reference to those reasons without reading the letter itself, though if that is desired I will read it in its entirety to make sure that I do not misinterpret what it says.
But just to give a precis of the reasons for the rejection, the first was because of what might be called the pocket development of the community. There are areas in Kitimat which are fairly well populated and developed, and there are also areas in Kitimat which are relatively sparsely populated. The town planners of Kitimat laid out the program of construction so that it would function in this

way, so there would be what you could call pocket development areas. Apparently this would entail a great deal more costly method of providing letter carrier service than if there was a large area of population such as there is, say, in the city of Ottawa, where there is block after block after block of dwellings.
The second reason was that the public transportation schedules there do not coincide, or did not at that time, with the times when transportation would be required by the letter carriers of the post office.
The third was that there is a substantial part of the population living in bunkhouses, staff houses or dormitories; that these people are not permanent residents, and that to provide a letter carrier service for them would mean that it would have to be discontinued when the dormitories or the staff houses closed down and the people moved out of the community because construction ceased or moved into permanent housing.
The fourth reason was that there was a very high level of employment at Kitimat and it would not be possible to recruit a suitable staff of letter carriers to keep it up to the necessary strength. I do not know whether this means that the salary structure in other employment would be sufficiently high to attract workers to a greater degree than would a lower salary schedule, but I imagine this is what it gets at.
Then finally, and I took issue with this as soon as I read it, it was stated that because of unusual climatic conditions in the area there would be considerable risk of interruption of delivery service during the winter months. I imagine the reference is to rain and snow. While it does rain in Kitimat, I do not think it rains any more there than in some of the other communities in that area.
These are the reasons given. I would like to point out that even though this was the initial objection there was not much validity to any of the five objections raised by the minister. In this regard I am sure the minister received communications from other individuals in Kitimat, although I do not know. However, because Kitimat was a new community and proceeded on a planned and orderly basis, it could be classified as pocket development, but I think in all fairness it is not too much different from any of these so-called suburban areas surrounding many of our larger cities today in which there are parks, playgrounds, shopping centres and an expanse of space between them. So this to me does not have that degree of validity which would warrant rejection of a letter carrier system, and it does not affect the distance a
Supply-Post Office
postman would have to walk. The neighbourhoods themselves are compact, and it is not much different from any of the modern suburban developments surrounding many of our cities.
With regard to the public transportation system in Kitimat, which everyone at that time admitted was not too good, the minister was sent a copy of the Kitimat bus schedule showing that buses ran continuously throughout the day from 7.05 a.m. until the last full through service at 7.35 in the evening. Then there were bus services following that time to selected areas. Throughout the day there was regular bus service from one end of the community to the other; and while it may not have been too good, it would not interfere in any way with the operations of a letter carrier. Now that we have these scooters perhaps you can disregard that point in any event.
The third point, as to there being a number of dormitories, staff houses, bunkhouses and so on has no validity either, because this was not considered in the initial request for letter carrier service by myself or the individuals concerned. The fact that they would be temporarily housed was not considered in the original request; we thought it should be excluded.
There was a high level of employment in Kitimat, but here I must draw a parallel between the city of Prince Rupert and Kitimat because we are in somewhat the same class, or were at that time, and have similar populations. The wage level in private industry in that city was comparable with Kitimat; but even if the high level of employment in Kitimat was used as an objection to establishing letter carrier service, I hope that does not imply that we need to have a large number of people unemployed before any sort of government services are established. Other than that I do not see what validity that argument has. If it was the wage level which was the deciding factor in engaging people, rather than their working for private industry, then it would seem to me that is a substantial and valid argument for increasing the salaries paid to letter carriers to make them comparable with industry.
The references to unusual climatic conditions, and so on, as I said are not too understandable because we have letter carrier service in Prince Rupert. I could file a great deal of information from the provincial department of agriculture, which conducts surveys of rainfall, snowfall and weather conditions throughout the communities, and I can say there is not too much difference between Prince Rupert and Kitimat so far as rain and snow are concerned. But the

Supply-Post Office
fact is that we have letter carrier delivery service in Prince Rupert but not in Kitimat.
Subsequent to these arguments being dispelled by additional correspondence which I had with the minister, I received a further communication from him. Again this is not classified as "personal and confidential", or at least there is no "personal and confidential" stamp on it. This was over a year ago and followed a detailed survey of Kitimat itself. This letter dealt exclusively with the number of points of call; the criterion used apparently is whether there will be a minimum of 2,500 points of call within what is called a compact, well-built area. That determines whether or not there will be a letter carrier service. At that time, in 1958, they were able to count only 2,240 calls at points where the necessary requirements were met. So there were 260 points of call less than the minimum number required.
Admittedly, since that time the construction program at Kitimat has been seriously curtailed. Some 1,700 or 1,800 construction employees were denied the right to work and continue the construction program at Kitimat. This dislocated the economy of Kitimat to a serious degree and resulted in many of the bunkhouses, staff houses and dormitories being closed, though I do not think that affected the over-all picture very much since these places were not included in the initial consideration which was given to this matter. It is true also that following the curtailment of construction the Aluminum Company of Canada proceeded to develop a more efficient system of production in the plant at Kitimat which resulted in a smaller number of people being employed to achieve the same volume of production. This also contributed to upsetting the economy of the area. Following this trend a number of vacancies occurred in the homes which had been built as permanent residences, and this state of affairs continued for a number of months.
However, I have been keeping in close touch with the development of the aluminum industry and the effect of this development on Kitimat. Gradually over the past few months there has been an increase in activity in the industry, up to a point where at the present time it is either in full production or close to full production having regard to the facilities available. There is once again an increase in community activity. Whether it is sufficient to make up for recent losses I do not know, but I think the most serious difficulties have been overcome and the effects of the economic collapse are being adjusted. Accordingly I think this would be a good time to consider making an additional investigation in order

to see whether a letter carrier service can be established in Kitimat in future.
It has been indicated to me that my time has just about expired, so I will conclude by leaving that particular question for the minister to deal with.

Mr. Chairman, in my area postal services have improved considerably in the last three years. There is one little problem I should like to take up, and it has to do with the town of Dalhousie, an important and expanding community where the International Paper Company has just announced a development project which will double the capacity of its mill at a cost of some $8 million.
The town of Campbellton as well as the city of Edmundston and other towns of similar size have daily delivery of mail, and I understand the Post Office Department has every intention of introducing a daily delivery service in Dalhousie. I was in Dalhousie about a month ago and a delegation came to me wanting to know why places such as Campbellton could have daily delivery service while places such as Dalhousie had to wait so long to get them. I feel sure the minister will take whatever steps are necessary in this direction.
Another point I wish to raise concerns mail delivery in Madawaska county, where residents have been waiting now for over a year for the introduction of rural route services. The reason given for the delay is that there are no boxes available, but with so many people in this country out of work that does not appear to me a very strong reason, beoause I am sure that boxes could easily and quickly be provided.
I was pleased to get a letter from the minister yesterday, and I may tell him that though it was marked "personal and confidential" I had it published in the local newspaper, containing as it did information that rural route delivery of mail would be inaugurated in St. Joseph beginning July 1. I thank the minister very much for giving such prompt consideration to this matter. I live in an area where people live four or five to what is called a range-

At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I was about to conclude my remarks when one o'clock came. The contractors who are awarded the

contracts to which I referred accept them in many cases with a considerable personal sacrifice to themselves because the prices at which they are obliged to bid in order to get the work do not always give them sufficient money to encourage them to give the additional little services that people have come to expect.
In many outlying areas you will have a few people-perhaps 5, 10 or 15 families- living along what is called a range, or in French, rang. The contractors will by-pass those families. I feel that is a practice that should not be tolerated. Although perhaps few in number those people should have an equal right to have their mail delivered to their doors when the rural route systems are established. When bids are being called I believe it would be an excellent idea to make it clear in the tender form that these little areas wherever they may be, have to be serviced.
I am pleased to note that the establishment of rural route services in areas such as mine has been speeded up. In many communities that are small in size it is not easy or possible to secure a responsible person to act as postmaster. The establishment of rural route service is an excellent trend.
I wish now to raise what I consider to be an important point and one concerning which I have received many complaints. I have always felt that when a merchant in a small town or village is appointed as postmaster he is given a competitive advantage over the other merchants in the community. This leads to abuses because people are obliged to go to the store in any event to cash their family allowance or pension cheques and to get their mail. Naturally the merchant who serves as postmaster has a knowledge of their affairs and can advance them credit because he knows when their cheques will come in. Because they are already in the store they may prefer to make their purchases there. I feel that the merchants who complain of this have a legitimate complaint. The establishment of rural route systems such as that to be inaugurated in St. Joseph in Madawaska county will to a great degree eliminate the practice that leads to the abuses I have just mentioned. I feel it is wrong to appoint a small town or village merchant as postmaster for the reasons I have stated.
In some areas, of course, our people do not like the idea of having rural route service. In some areas the people prefer it over all other systems of service. I have in my riding a very fine community called Tidehead. They want a post office. It is a rather large community and it could serve as headquarters for the rural route mail for many communities
Supply*-Post Office
adjoining Tidehead. I feel that more consideration should be given to the feelings of the people who live in the small communities. If they want a post office let us give them one and if they want rural route service let us see that they have it. I feel that the post office has to look on this enterprise as does any other business that is trying to give satisfaction to the people. In attempting to give that satisfaction the department should attempt to accommodate people in every way possible. I see no reason why we should wait any longer for daily delivery from door to door by carrier service in the town of Dal-housie.
In saying these things I also wish to congratulate the Postmaster General who has been extremely co-operative with me in anything I have had to do with his department. I can assure hon. members that the service has always been very speedy. I shall expect to see the points I have raised corrected and I am confident they will be. I am grateful for the opportunity of bringing these matters to the attention of the committee.
Mr. Chairman, when I look across the aisle and see the minister of socialist enterprise-
object immediately.

-memory opens the door to the near past. It seems such a short time ago that the present minister sat on the opposition benches pouring sulphurous language in a mellifluous voice over the head of the former postmaster general. We who have been here for some time have seen the evolution of a near rebel in opposition to a responsible minister. The hon. member for Port Arthur said, "A complete metamorphosis", and I think that is an excellent term because the minister has come out of his chrysalis. History repeats itself and advancing age and increased responsibility have had this mellowing effect. That is part of the democratic system.
The minister is doing a good job. He is doing many of the things for which he condemned the former minister and doing them in the same way. However, he has used hn imagination and put new life into the department. I appreciate the courtesy with which he has dealt with any problems I have brought to his attention and the promptitude with which he has dealt with matters I have discussed. I give the minister full credit for industry, activity and imagination so far as the Post Office Department is concerned.
However, the minister has caused me at times an unnecessary amount of thought and labour because in reply to all my correspondence he marks it "personal and confidential",

Supply-Post Office
even if it is just a question of putting a new rail up on the village post office steps. I bring this up because I know other hon. members have been caused a tremendous amount of extra work, and he has overburdened many of us with this practice. I wonder whether there is some unknown recondite reason for the practice which we call the personal and confidential technique.
I want to show the committee what unnecessary work it is causing us. In order to do that I am going to read a letter. The name of the recipient of this letter is purely fictitious. It is not intended to refer to any person either living or dead. However, the subject matter of the letter represents in two or three paragraphs the kind of letters I have had to write to my constituents because I receive letters from the minister all marked "personal and confidential". This is a typical letter.
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry, but I know the hon. member does not want to break the rules of the house. He will find a citation in the rules which prohibits the reading of imaginary letters.
Pardon me; I have in effect changed only the name. The letter is composite in form.

Is
this one complete letter exactly as received from the department?

This is a letter I have composed as a result of my experience. The letter is addressed to:
Captain, The Honourable Algernon Claude Hamilton, Old Cove, British Columbia Re: Derelicton of duty,
Postmaster, Old Cove, B.C.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is completely out of order in reading imaginary letters.
No.

speechtext: I would ask the Postmaster General to refer me to the rule because it seems to me if the letter was written by the hon. member it would be the same thing as if it were part of his speech.
The only thing you could accuse him of would be reading his speech.

Mr. Chairman, I am reading this letter to indicate the type of letter I have to write because every letter I receive from the Postmaster General is marked "personal and confidential". I think I am entitled to present my point of view and support my argument with this illustration. I know of no rule in the book which prevents
[Mr. Herridge.)
my reading a letter which illustrates the correspondence I am required to write. May I continue, Mr. Chairman?

If the
hon. member has something else to say I suggest that he say it and in the meantime I shall find the rule in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms.
I am not going to be put off easily in that way.
Go ahead, read the letter.

Maybe the Postmaster General is referring to citation 158 on page 134 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, which reads as follows:

Does this meet the point the minister has in mind. I doubt whether on this citation I can draw the line that the Postmaster General has indicated. If the hon. member who is speaking says that it is the kind of letter that he himself has written, or that he is supposed to have written from time to time, I do not think this citation would apply. To my way of thinking this means a letter written by some other hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for finding me the citation from your more adequate references. It is exactly the one I was looking for. It says:
It is against the general principles which govern debate to read to the house-
This is what the hon. member is intending to do.
-an imaginary letter-[DOT]
He has already said that is what it is.
-supposed to have been written by one of the sitting members of parliament.
I am a sitting member of parliament at the present time and the hon. member is ascribing the letter to me.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member has indicated that the letter he wished to quote is one that he would write or that he ordinarily writes to one of his constituents, and not a letter from the Postmaster General, if I heard him correctly.

This is purely the type of letter I am required to write because of this personal and confidential technique. I will now proceed with the letter:

My dear Algernon:
I have discussed the contents of your letter of March 1, last, with the appropriate person. However, it would not be what is played at Lords to divulge his name.
Before proceeding with your complaint, I shall answer your query as to what sort of a chap the Postmaster General is. While from your point of view he wears the wrong coloured tie, and has been known to enter the House of Commons in a vest of style and colour that would cause you some dismay, I must, in fairness, say his heart is in the right place, he is most industrious and his unconventional vests do indicate an imagination that I think has had a beneficial effect on the administration since he took office.
Now to your complaint. The letter I have received from the appropriate person is marked "personal and confidential". Therefore, I find it necessary to write allegorically and all I can say is that with my knowledge of the appropriate person's ability to smell a rat when he sees it hovering in the air, and later to nip it in the bud, I am confident that the administrative "dry-rot" you brought to my attention will be lopped off in due course, to your complete satisfaction.
While you may convey the information contained in this letter to this village post office patrons, on no account disclose the source of your information. However, you have my permission to say it came from an authoritative but undisclosed Ottawa source.
Trusting I have made the situation quite clear in a personal and confidential way, I remain
Your old Comrade-in-Arms.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I think we ought to have the correspondence completed. I wonder whether we can have the reply to that letter filed? I simply want it because I want to see what a member of parliament looks like when he starts writing letters to himself.
For purposes of information may I ask the erudite member how one smells a rat hovering in the air and nips it in the bud.

I can answer that. I have used that allegorical statement as a result of reading a Conservative member's remarks made in the British House of Commons in 1876.
I have drawn this to the minister's attention and I am sure he will reconsider this technique because, mind you, in addition to marking it "personal and confidential" he sends a tissue copy of his letter. I do not know what to do with it. I have not been able to find any use for it to date. I do hope the minister will find his way clear to change his technique.
When I receive a letter marked "personal and confidential" I treat it as personal and confidential, but I do wish the personal and confidential would apply to, shall I say, strictly confidential matters and I do not mind when necessary on personal matters. I would ask the minister to comment on this question when he replies. I am not the only
Supply-Post Office
one who has suffered from this practice. Members on the government side have also expressed their adverse opinion of it. As a matter of fact, this is one of the major criticisms this afternoon.
Having said that, I now proceed. As I see it, a member's responsibilities when it comes to discussing estimates are two in number. The first is to deal with the policies of the department in general, if he has any criticism of same, and the second is to bring to the attention of the committee any particular problem that concerns his constituents, and that is what most members do when they discuss estimates.
Before I proceed with a few remarks about general policy, I wish to say in all sincerity, because we hear some sections of the civil service criticized on occasions, that the Canadian people are very fortunate in having an excellent, efficient and first-class staff in the Post Office Department from the deputy minister right down through the administrative level. We accept this service daily without realizing the planning and consideration that has to go into the distribution of mail in Canada to the satisfaction of the public every day of the year. I think we should recognize that fact. Any matters I have brought to the attention of the minister or his senior officials have always been approached from the point of view that people would adopt who are operating a successful socialist enterprise for the public advantage.
With respect to the staff throughout the country we should also recognize the very good service that is rendered by the many people in the more humble positions. The service goes on day after day and is accepted just as we accept the work of the tracklayer on the railways in carrying out his monotonous daily task so that we may travel with speed and in comfort. I hope that the minister will use all his influence to see that the excellent services rendered by post office staffs and postmen tramping their beats are recognized by adequate increases in their salaries to conform with the increased cost of living.
I have a few other matters to bring to the minister's attention. A constituent of mine wrote me about a question that concerns civil rights. I wrote the minister about it and I have his reply here but I cannot quote it because it is marked "personal and confidential". I think the gentleman who wrote me has a point. The minister in writing to me indicated that he thought-how shall I put it-in view of it being marked confidential that he had made the implicit

Supply-Post Office
explicit, but I cannot agree. That is all I
can say at the present time. In any event,
this gentleman wrote me and said:

I would appreciate any information that is available on a matter which offhand I would consider as coming under civil rights. I am not familiar with what category my subject would come under other than civil rights.
Now as I understand, under our form of government the individual can live a private life, his business being his own in so far as the general public is concerned as long as he abides by the law. We have to fill out forms for income taxes, we give certain information for voters' lists, answer questions when we take on employment with a firm; we also give the post office our name and our address and we as in my case rent a box with a number from said post office. Now I would take from this that the information given each of the above is strictly for their own use and not for release to the general public.
Now it has come to my attention that a person can purchase from any post office in Canada for the sum of $2 a list of citizens that gives their name, address in the area which they choose to have knowledge of. I do not think this is the correct thing to do. The post office is a government agency and should not be used as an information bureau.
He goes on to say:
I would go to the post office and inquire, and the only answer was that if I put a stamp on it and mailed it they would see it got to the party.
He is referring to when he went to the post office to inquire about a person's address.
In short they were not allowed to divulge a person's mailing address. I can see the wisdom to this; they in those years respected the privacy of the individual. This present system leaves you open to a shower of phony advertising literature and such, it may be lucrative to the post office but the post office is supposed to be a very private business. I think stern measures should be taken to tighten up and attend to the business of handling mail and nothing in the way of as I said before of being an information bureau for a $2 bill.
I think my correspondent has a point there. He says he has gone to the post office and asked for the address of a person and has been told that if he will put a stamp on the letter they will supply the address and forward it but will not give the address. At the same time apparently a commercial company by paying $2	can get a	list	of	thepatrons of a certain	post office	and	on	the
basis of that list distribute their advertising literature. Personally I think my correspondent has a point. I promised him to raise the question on the estimates of the Post Office Department and I should like the minister to deal with it briefly when he replies to the eulogies and criticisms from the opposition benches.
I have one other	suggestion	and	it	hasto do with stamps. I must say	that	on	the
whole I think there has been an improvement in the design and quality of the stamps issued by the Post Office Department since 
the minister came into office. But I do suggest that possibly there could be considerable improvement if there was an opportunity provided for Canadians living in all sections of Canada and having various backgrounds and aptitudes to make some contribution to the design of these stamps. I suggest it would be a good idea to have some form of competition for Canadian artists who do this kind of work so that the minister's selection will not be confined to a few professionals who submit designs but will be made on as wide a base of talent in this direction as Canada can provide.
I have also been asked to mention to the minister that some remarkable subjects for stamp design are to be found in the Kootenays. There is the Kootenay-Columbia district, the Indians and their particularly interesting chiefs, the Thompson period, the Hudson Bay period, the stern-wheel steamers and various well known characters in mining, lumbering and agriculture. I have been asked to mention that because we in the Kootenay district are under the impression that we have not received due recognition from several of the government departments, including the Post Office Department, that go in for illustrating certain books and stamps.
I come now to the local and the concrete. The residents of Rossland were very pleased when the Department of Public Works decided to build a new post office.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he not think that the present member for Kootenay West is perhaps a qualified person to be considered as a subject for a stamp design?

I welcome the hon. member's fine suggestion but 1 have always understood that high rank and station and great contributions to the state should not be recognized until the person is dead. As a matter of fact, I would rather have a new post office or two while I am alive. The people of Rossland were very pleased when it was decided to build a new post office. The first recommendation was to renovate the old one. After going through the building it was my personal opinion that it would be a waste of money, that it would cost a great deal more to renovate the old building than was anticipated, and once again, as usual, the member for Kootenay West was correct. The public works staff reinvestigated the whole situation and it was decided finally to build a new post office. I hope that every effort will be made to meet the responsible persons in Rossland such as members of the city council and representatives of the chamber of commerce and other organizations so that

the new post office will be located in the very best site possible to serve the interests of Rossland people. I understand this building is now being given consideration and will be undertaken next year.
I also want to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General the necessity of the officials in his department watching developments in the Kootenay district closely, particularly the need of changes at times in rural routes. There is one district where there were only five people a few years ago and at the present time there are 1,000. The development in the district is causing changes that will require adjustment in the service given. I cannot think of any drastic or particular one at the present time but I bring the matter to the minister's attention because of the changes occurring from increases in population, the building of new highways, the introduction of new bus services and transportation services and so on.
I come now to a problem that concerns the little village that is closest to where I live, namely the not well known but well situated and beautiful village of Nakusp. The chamber of commerce, the women's institute and the organizations there have been concerned in the last year or two about the time it takes to get mail from Vancouver into our district. The time is such that on occasion business people are required to use the long distance telephone much more than would be necessary if the mail service was a bit faster. It has been suggested that the minister's officials give consideration to the bus leaving Nelson a few hours later than it leaves at the present time so that it can bring mail there after the plane arrives at Castlegar in the afternoon. I mention this matter because of complaints and ask the minister to have it checked.
The minister knows that for some years I have urged the necessity of a postal bag from Revelstoke to Nakusp and distribution from there to all points south as far as Edgewood. I know the minister's officials investigated the situation and found that the volume of mail was somewhat small. I was very surprised to hear the cost of handling this bag in view of the fact that it is a government ferry that runs from Arrowhead to Nakusp and mail is brought up from Revelstoke to Arrowhead on contract. I thought it would cost a dollar a day or something of that sort. I cannot see any reason for the expense that was indicated by the report I received. However, I will let that matter rest at the present time.
I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that a new highway is being built now and that it is likely that in the future there will be a bus running from Revelstoke

south to Nelson via Nakusp. I urge that the officials of the department watch these developments so that they can take advantage of these changed transportation circumstances as soon as possible after they occur.
I have had one or two other complaints, although this is a minor one. In a number of places I have been informed that the rural mail list is often incomplete or inaccurate as to the address concerned or as to occupation. I suppose the minister does not live as close to the rank and file as do I. I live among the people. I am not in an exalted position. However, I hear what the ordinary person has to say about public affairs.
Mr. Chairman, I not only live among the people; I am one of the people.

I am glad to hear that. I am glad to know the minister is human. With regard to those sitting on the government benches there have been a few cases where I doubted that. However, even in a thing like an incorrect occupation, dissatisfaction can be caused. I had a gentleman come to me who is manager of a lumberyard, and he was down in the post office directory from year to year as a labourer. A person's occupation should be correctly stated. I have had a few of these cases brought to my attention. I urge that the local postmasters should be asked to check these lists; and not just send the old list in annually but to check the list carefully and to make certain that the address and the occupation of every patron is correct. That is not a very socialist suggestion but I represent all the people of Kootenay West. This suggestion comes from some of my Conservative friends but I am quite willing to advance it when they elect me as their representative to serve all the people.
I have one more suggestion to make, and it is my last one. I have received a few letters complaining of the low pay of the casual help employed in the larger post offices such as those in Trail and Nelson. I have also had letters from a few other points dealing with the situation in general. If my information is correct, it appears to me that the pay received by casual help in British Columbia for work in the post office on certain occasions is very much below the prevailing rates; in fact I am informed in some cases it is 50 per cent of the prevailing rate. When the Department of Public Works lets a contract in a district the contractor must agree to pay prevailing rates. I suggest that consideration be given to the prevailing rates in any district when casual help is being employed.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I once again want to emphasize this fact. Tremendous

Supply-Post Office
progress is taking place in Kootenay West. Tremendous developments are in sight and expansion is going on now at a rapid rate, and it will continue to go on in this garden of Eden in Canada. I urge that the minister's officials keep a close watch on these developments and these changing situations so that they will be ready at the first opportunity to adjust, rearrange or increase the services that are now provided so that they will continue to provide the efficient service that we have enjoyed throughout the years.

In common with other hon. members who have made some comment on the estimates of the Postmaster General, I should like to commence by complimenting him and his department on the excellent services they have been giving. Representing as I do a riding which is mainly rural and which has a number of rural routes and small post offices, I find that a great deal of the work I have to do relates to the Post Office Department. I must say that with very few exceptions I have received very good service and have been able to give good service to those people who wrote to me with problems or complaints.
There are just two matters which I should like to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General and the officials this afternoon. The first one relates to the tender system for rural routes. As we all know, the present system is-and I think properly so-that the lowest tenderer on the rural route is awarded the job. I think this is a fair system to be undertaken. However, I have found a number of difficulties that I think should be carefully considered by the department. In a number of cases there is evidence that a contractor or a proposed contractor will make a bid which is excessively low, much lower than that of all the other people who have bid. I feel that sometimes the person who has made this low bid has not done so properly. He may have one of three reasons for making an extremely low bid. The first one is that he may have wanted to eliminate all the other competition on the route and then hope to come back to the department in two years and get an increase back to what he should have had in the first place. In a number of cases I think there is definite evidence that people have put in ridiculously low bids and they go along just on the expectation they will apply and get an increase later on.
Another reason that this thing happens is that the person is incapable of estimating his job properly. The third is that he may not be properly equipped and that although he is able to give an estimate, he may do a poor job. After all, he is carrying the royal mail and the person who is selected ought to have

proper equipment and ought to be able to give good service. My request to the Postmaster General is that in cases where he receives a bid which is quite low in comparison with other tenders he should make an independent investigation to see whether the person who is bidding is actually the proper person for doing the job and capable of carrying the mail in a satisfactory way.
The second matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention concerns the urban mail delivery service in the town of Parry Sound. This has been one of the matters that the residents of that town have been requesting for some years. They have a post office which has sufficient revenue for mail delivery service door to door. They are just a little short of the number of persons required for mail delivery service. A check was made within the past year and at first it was thought that there were enough people, but subsequently it turned out on a re-check that there were not enough. It has been drawn to my attention that people who were potential customers were not counted for some reason or other as householders, and I therefore urge the Postmaster General to have a further check made as soon as possible of the number of householders qualified to receive mail to see if a few extra people can be found so that mail delivery can be provided to this town, which is actually increasing very rapidly each year in population and industry.
With those two matters and the compliments I gave to the Postmaster General I should just like to add that as regards the rural mail delivery services particularly the department has given very good co-operation in any extension of rural mail routes where requested, and they have stretched their regulations to the limit in lots of cases in order to give good mail delivery service.
