Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) stated earlier, it cannot be said that the present Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) is doing much worse than his predecessor, but we are always surprised to find that the former critic of the Post Office Department did not introduce the changes he was suggesting when he was in the opposition.
However, what struck me most, and what amused me particularly in the minister's introductory statement on his departmental estimates, is his remarks about visiting post offices at all hours of the day or night and noting the cheerfulness of postal workers.

That part of his speech struck me for two reasons. In the first place, it is rather unusual for a Postmaster General to go about post offices by day and by night to check on the cheerfulness of his staff. It is somewhat outside the bounds of logic.
Then again, does not the minister trust his employees? If he does not, well let him replace them, and let him tell us his reasons for doing so, namely that they are incompetent.
A minister going through post offices at two or three in the morning to check up on the cheerfulness of his personnel, that is really laughable.
Besides, I note that the minister is laughing just now. He might well do so, because if he had thought twice, he would not have said that.
The minister said he noted the cheerfulness of the staff.
Well, he must have made his visits at the wrong hours, because I have been meeting large numbers of post office employees, and civil servants generally-particularly people working outdoors-and I can assure you their mood is not so cheerful as that.
If there is one minister who is being criticized by his staff at this time for his lack of action, it is certainly the Postmaster General.
His employees have been trying to get raises for their colleagues. Raises have been granted to 50,000 employees, but not to postal workers. In fact, postal workers seem to have been placed at the bottom of the list.
Would the hon. member allow me a question?
Certainly.
Could the hon. member cite a single case in support of his statements to the house?
It is not my practice to reveal my sources of information, because I would not want government employees to be penalized for daring to talk to a Liberal member.
Would the hon. member-
If my hon. friend would get out of his hole in the ground, he might find a good many dissatisfied people in his own constituency. Besides, it is a matter of common knowledge.
That is not true, and that is no answer.

You only have to take a look at the civil servants' newspaper to see how
Supply-Post Office
much dissatisfaction there is, and in the same paper, you will see the complaints of postal employees, who are of course dissatisfied with their present situation, because the raises to which they are entitled are being held up.
All we have to do is to look around and see what is going on. Members of parliament should not be asked to give their sources of information; it could only mean trouble for those who gave out the information. I know there is discontent, and especially people are wondering whether the delay in granting postal workers the raise they were promised is not meant as a punishment for those who have been waging the great battle for salary increases. They were the ones who carried the battle, and it now seems as if someone is out to punish them for it; in fact they will probably be the last to get the promised raise. If there are people in fact, who really fought the great battle for civil service salary increases-
Please be responsible, be responsible.

Mr. Chairman, would you tell that thing over there to shut up? I am sick and tired of my hon. friend's interventions. In the matter of irresponsibility, I have never seen the like of him.
I wonder whether this delay in granting the requested increases is not a punishment inflicted on postal workers. In fact not only will they not get their increases immediately but, judging from the present attitude of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) there will be no retroactivity, whether they get their raise in two or three days, or in a month, they will not benefit from the retroactivity granted to the 50,000 who already got their increase in April.
They stand to lose hundreds of thousands of dollars because they waged the battle to help Canadian civil servants who were ill paid, particularly since the election of the present government.
The present minister may have fine qualities, he may have great accomplishments to his credit, but he certainly slipped in failing to insist on salary increases for the people who deliver the mail day in and day out, rain or shine, summer and winter, under extremes of hot and cold weather, carrying heavy bags to serve the public. I think those people deserved a better deal than they have received.
The minister, who introduced the use of scooters in his department, also referred to small carts that are being put to the test,

Supply-Post Office
similar to those used to carry golf clubs. I have had the opportunity to discuss this with a few mail carriers, and their reaction was that the idea was absolutely unthinkable and that, for all practical purposes, they could not accept them. They have been wondering whether the minister was thinking of using this new device to throw an additional load on the already overburdened workers and thus cut down the staff.
Why not buy them a horse and cart, as used by bread and milk salesmen who do not travel very fast and go from door to door.
In my view, Mr. Chairman, postal employees have certainly not received the consideration they deserved from their minister, and I hope that when their raises do come- as they are bound to eventually-the minister will see that they be retroactive to April 1, as in the case of the first 50,000 who got their raises. Then, perhaps, they might be able to believe that the minister has really looked after his departmental staff.
I do not want to take too much time, because I would hate to be accused of delaying the Post Office Department's estimates, but there is one thing I should like to submit to the minister. It is known that the city of Hull has been expanding considerably, and that, in addition to the old section on the eastern side of Brewers creek we now have a new section on the western side, which already has grown larger than the old.
The post office has a sort of little nook there where mail carriers go and fetch the mail they have to deliver. Furthermore, boxes have to be installed on street corners, from which mail carriers may pick up additional mail for delivery. That area includes four important districts, that is Tetreau, Wright, Lafontaine and Dollard. Consequently, it would be necessary and urgent that the Post Office Department build another post office there which would, first of all, allow mail carriers to pick up their bagful of mail; at the same time we would be rid of those horrible boxes that stand on street corners, especially in the most developed areas, which are so picturesque.
Mr. Chairman, several members have already referred to that mania of the Postmaster General's of writing "personal and confidential" letters. Besides, you know very well that a letter is not necessarily of a personal and confidential nature just because its sender has chosen to write in those words at the top of the sheet. To be genuinely so, such letters must be of a personal and confidential character. In fact, I will quote one

of them, even, if it is not considered delicate to do so. It is a letter which is in no way of a personal or confidential character, and I wrote to the minister to tell him that I did not consider it as such. Furthermore, after having advised the minister, I sent a copy of it to the persons concerned and I had a right to, because it was in no way of a personal or confidential character. Under the circumstances, I was fully justified to do what I did. Here is the letter referred to:
Personal and confidential Dear Mr. Caron:
This is in reference to your letter of May 10, in which you ask that letter carrier service be established in Gatineau.
An inquiry to establish whether Gatineau meets the required conditions for mail carrier service has just been completed. The matter is still under consideration but no decision has yet been taken. I am sorry 1 am unable to give you a definite answer at this time, but I hope to be in a position to do so in the near future.
Sincerely,
William Hamilton, Postmaster General.
Can anyone look upon that letter as being a personal and confidential letter? Is the minister out to prevent members of parliament from transmitting to their constituents the news they get from departments? I do not know. I would not like to accuse the minister unfairly, but I am inclined to believe that there is something there which borders on mania. I would ask him, whenever he wants a letter to be personal and confidential, to include in it facts that are genuinely of a personal and confidential nature. However, as everyone knows, letters such as the one I have just read are not of a personal or confidential character.
I have another one of the same type, in which there is absolutely nothing of a personal and confidential character-I do not want to take time to read it-and in which the minister advises me that the matter does not come under his department; and he adds:
I am sending a copy of your letter to the Minister of Public Works.
Is there anything personal and confidential in those two letters?
I ask the minister to change his ways by sending us replies that will allow us to supply information to those concerned.
I shall now revert to the subject of door to door delivery in Gatineau. The population of this town numbers 13,000 at present. Some people have to travel one and a half miles

to get their mail and post their letters. The minister will perhaps claim that he is following the established practice. I admit that this was probably the practice followed in the past, but I remember that when he was on this side of the house, the present Potsmaster General urged the government to bring about all necessary changes. He is now holding that office and it is his own responsibility. If changes had to be made when he was in the opposition, why does he not make them now that he is in a position to do so?
It will be claimed perhaps that the population is not high enough and that the volume of business is not such as to justify the building of a post office. The reason for this is obvious enough. Deprived of proper facilities, those people deal with the Hull or Ottawa post office, and the local post office pays the piper. If proper service was provided, we would have the required volume of business.
Moreover, even with door to door delivery, people would have to go to the post office to purchase postage stamps. Stamp distribution centres should be established in various places for this purpose. Nothing is easier than to allow certain grocers or merchants to sell postage stamps and enable the public to purchase the stamps they need. In this way, the volume of business of the Gatineau post office would reach the required figure.
Moreover, the minister would have made one of the improvements he was asking for when he was sitting on this side of the house.
Well, I remind him of the past, of the great improvements he used to ask for, in short, I ask him to remember everything he said when he was on this side. For instance, he stated that postal service should be available to the public, that it was a public service and that the reason for the existence of the Post Office Department was the public.
I am asking him for the same thing. Let him carry out what he suggested. Let him make the postal system available to the people who need it, by making a few changes and a few improvements. Even if it is impossible to have a door to door delivery service immediately, let there be, at least, some letter boxes, and a few merchants should be allowed to sell stamps, so that people who want to post their letters will not have to walk one and a half miles to do so.
I must say that, as far as Gatineau Point is concerned, I submitted the matter to the

minister who received me very courteously -I have to admit that the minister is always urbane when we approach him-and I asked him to have the post office enlarged. I should like to take this opportunity to make one or two remarks. As the representative of a fast-growing community in western Canada I should like to draw certain matters to the attention of the Postmaster General. I hasten to assure the hon. gentleman that my words are not words of criticism but of constructive suggestion and, later on, there may even be words of commendation.
The municipality of Burnaby has a population of some 100,000 and an area of 40 square miles. Yet Burnaby is without its own central post office. New Westminster and Vancouver have complete postal facilities. If consideration is being given to the establishment of a federal building in central Burnaby I would suggest the location be in the vicinity of our municipal hall. I feel that consideration should be given to the establishment of a post office for Burnaby.
I also suggest that the Postmaster General give attention to the idea of having a Burnaby postmark. I realize that these things are perhaps relatively insignificant in the view of other hon. members of the committee but

Supply-Post Office
anyone who realizes the pride of a municipality or city will realize the importance of the suggestions I am advancing.
In forwarding these suggestions I feel I should also bring to the minister's attention the fact that there is discussion in the Vancouver area concerning the metropolitaniza-tion of the whole area. I would point out that Burnaby is the heart of the lower mainland, the geographic centre of the mainland of lower British Columbia. I think he should give consideration to the long range possibilities of the establishment of a post office in the Burnaby area. In the last 20 years the population of Burnaby has risen from 50,000 to 100,000 within an area of 40 square miles and with the present dynamic leadership being given in the community not only by the municipal council but by the board of trade there is every indication that the population will perhaps double again in the next 10 or 15 years.
I wish also to direct the minister's attention to a similar situation existing in the municipality of Richmond which I also represent. Strangely enough the population of this area also doubled in the last 20 years. Richmond has a present population, I believe, of 40,000 and covers an area of 57 square miles. I would point out that all airmail from the Vancouver area goes through Richmond because the Vancouver international air port is located there. I wonder if the minister would also give consideration to the establishment of a central post office in Richmond. We would like to see it located in the federal building in that area.
From time to time I understand that the Postmaster General receives certain complaints. I am at times critical when I feel that criticism is justified but I should like to point out to the minister that since my election in 1958 I have had occasion to bring to his attention only three or four complaints regarding the postal service in my riding. I have no hesitation in saying that in each instance the minister had the situation thoroughly investigated and in every case I received a satisfactory reply.
I wish to express appreciation to the minister for his being of assistance to me in another matter. Some criticism appeared in the local newspapers in my riding concerning the postal service in the area. I thought perhaps the criticism was not based on fact. The minister was kind enough to make arrangements under which I was able to take the four local editors from Burnaby and Richmond on a tour of the Vancouver post office. They were able to ask any questions they wished and an effort was made to explain anything which caused them difficulty.
[Mr. Drysdale.l
Since that time I have seen no criticism editorially in those newspapers.
Having worked in post offices during Christmas vacations I have developed a first hand approach to the subject of this department based on my experience as a letter carrier and sorter of mail. I am amazed at the few mistakes that are made by the post offices. I feel that some hon. members in presenting the complaints they have received magnify the minor mistakes that have been made. I would suggest that this is out of all proportion. The minister's department is probably subject to attack more than any other department for the reason that through every letter, post card and circular the Postmaster General representatively goes into the homes of Canadians. If there is any delay in the receipt of good news or bad or any minor delay in mail delivery we tend to ascribe the difficulties to the Postmaster General.
In studying the situation in my area and in attempting to bring problems or complaints to the attention of local departmental officials in both Vancouver and Burnaby I have found a genuine interest on their part in correcting any of the real or alleged delays. A suggestion was made to me which I will pass on because it may be valuable to other hon. members. When a person complains about delay in receiving a letter I am always pleased if they send me the particular letter so that I can then trace it and assist in discovering the reason for the delay. This provides the post office officials with an opportunity to clear up the difficulty.
I appreciate having had this opportunity to bring forward these few points which I know will be of interest to my constituents and to commend the minister on the excellent job he is doing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks concerning problems of general interest relative to the question of good relationships between the Post Office Department and the public. I feel this is of importance because this department more than any other department of government is in daily contact with Canadian citizens through the postal services.
I have a file of letters here. All the numerous communications I have had with the minister's department have been dealt with courteously but the replies have been marked "personal and confidential" and therefore it will be difficult for me to deal with some of the problems I have in mind.
The first problem with which I wish to deal concerns the amalgamation of the city of Sudbury. Amalgamations are a common occurrence today and have taken place not

only in Sudbury but elsewhere in Ontario. A part of my riding was amalgamated with the city of Sudbury and this has created a problem for the postal department. I am proud of the fact that the amalgamation took place but the residents of the area affected are entitled to expect the same postal services that are provided elsewhere in the municipality. I realize that this cannot be done immediately and I know that the local officials in Sudbury are investigating the matter of adequate postal services in this area. I appreciate, too, that this situation developed shortly after the government took office. I know that the personnel of the department in Sudbury are making every effort to have action taken on the question.
I feel that in instances like this the Post Office Department should take the initiative in having special studies made. A lack of action in this respect creates poor public relations between the department and the local citizens. I urge the minister to have a study made as rapidly as possible. If this were done it would reduce the number of complaints that are sent to members of parliament and the Postmaster General. People write to us because they have no one else to whom they can address their complaints. I appreciate very much receiving those complaints. It is their right to make the complaints and it is my duty to listen to them. I am certainly willing to receive them and pass them on to the minister on every occasion.
In this area, of course, some people have rural service only. Under the amalgamation the area became part of the greater city of Sudbury. Therefore, the people feel that they should receive door to door service promptly. Based on the population of the subdivision of this area, they should receive it.
Without quoting the actual words of the letters of the Postmaster General, his last letter simply indicated to me that the investigation which he told me was going on a month or two before had not even begun. This is the type of thing I find very hard to explain to my constituents, and it is difficult for them to feel satisfied with the approach of the minister to this problem. This is not an absolutely grave complaint but it is a proper one. I am sure the minister will realize that if there is a change in the community life and his department is affected he should make absolutely sure that he has the staff in the field to take care of the change. Possibly the personnel in the Sudbury area are overloaded with work; possibly they cannot find the time to make the investigation which is required to rearrange certain routes
Supply-Post Office
and give to the citizens the postal service which will be as good as that formerly given to the limited city of Sudbury. The citizens could be notified as soon as it is done, or they should be told that it will be done shortly. If that were done they would realize that it is not possible to make the change and rearrange the postal services in a few weeks or a month. If the matter is long delayed, especially as we were advised that the investigation which we were told was going on had not even begun some months after, the people should be informed about it.
I think it is proper that the minister should be advised that a rapid study of the problem should be made. The acuteness of the problem was known to his department, no doubt, long before this amalgamation application. I know that the one in Sudbury was discussed for at least three or four years. The citizens knew in advance that the amalgamation would take place on January 1 the following year. The department should have known that and that was the time to make the study. I am not saying that the amalgamation took place five years ago; I am saying that the application was made five years ago and the amalgamation took place since the present Postmaster General took office. Therefore he has the previous experience to know something about it and also he has the facilities since he became the Postmaster General.

Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege for me to speak on behalf of my constituency of St. Boniface, not to make complaints but to express my commendation of and thanks for the service given to the people of St. Boniface in the new area of Windsor Park, by granting them door to door service. In Charleswood we had door to door service last year, and this year we have received the drop rate of four cents on mail. We tried hard to obtain the four cent rate for the town of Transcona, and this month it has also been extended to that town. It has also been extended to places as far away as 10 miles from the city of St. Boniface, such as the village of St. Norbert and Fort Whyte, St. Charles, Pacific Junction, Tod post office in the municipality of St. Vital, and Birds Hill.
It is remarkable how well the people have been served since 1957. The year 1957 was the first time there was an improvement in that district by having a door to door delivery in the town of Transcona. Now the whole district, the metropolitan area of greater Winnipeg, has received the four cent rate.
I should like to thank the minister, his department and also the employees in the city of St. Boniface very much for their cooperation and their faithful service in the conduct of their duties.
There is another improvement that is being planned, namely the new post office for the city of St. Boniface. I understand this building will conform with the improvements in a city of 35,000 people which is growing fast, and it will harmonize with all the wonderful buildings that the city of St. Boniface is already blessed with. As you know, the city of St. Boniface is one of the oldest cities west of the capital. It has a French speaking population, is a city of culture and has wonderful buildings. I am sure the new building will conform to the present architectural style and the importance of such a city.
I should like to make one request. I believe the Post Office Department should issue

a stamp to commemorate the religious character of Christmas and counteract the emphasis on commercialism. I know that the Post Office Department has issued many worthy stamps to commemorate different historic events and I think the department should not forget to commemorate the nativity, the greatest event so far as Christianity throughout the world is concerned. I am sure this will be done. I do not want to take more time as many hon. members wish to speak. I have nothing but thanks to offer to the minister and his department.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to speak very long on this subject today but there are two or three matters I should like to raise at this time. The first, and certainly one of the most important that the minister should consider, is the pay and remuneration of the letter carriers. I think the rate of pay these men are receiving is disgraceful. I know that other speakers have referred to the yeoman service they render in all kinds of weather and certainly that is even more applicable in the area from which I come. The letter carriers have to go out when the temperature is 35, 40, 45 or 50 degrees below zero and sometimes have to wade through a couple of feet of snow that has fallen during the night. To me it is wonderful how they can even carry on their work. Certainly their rate of pay is in no way commensurate with the duties they perform for the public.
I have known some cases where letter carriers, after building up a few year's seniority in the department, have endeavoured to build themselves homes and when they came to pay the bills they found they had to leave the department, thus losing their seniority and all their benefits, and go back to work in the mines for a period of five years or so until they had reduced their mortgages before they could go back to the work of their choice in the department. I think it is a disgrace that they should lose all of their back benefits and I suggest that the minister should look into the matter very carefully and see if something cannot be done.
There is another small matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond said, while it may not be of vital national importance it certainly is important to the people in the particular area of my riding. I refer to the condition of the present post office premises in the combined towns of Ramore and Holtyre. The building is certainly not intended for this type of work. It cannot be expanded, and if the minister's

inspectors would go there I think they certainly would agree with the local people that there is a very great need for a new postal building to serve these two communities.
There is one other matter that has been brought to my attention by more than one person and has to do with what is possibly a policy of the minister's department. To illustrate the point I should like to refer to the remarks of the minister when he first introduced his estimates on May 27. As found at the bottom of page 4282 of Hansard, he said at that time:
In any organization as large as the Post Office Department the relations between management and staff are of critical importance.
I am glad to see that the minister realizes the importance of good relations between the employees and the employer, particularly in an undertaking as important as our postal service. As found in the second column on the same page he went on to say:
During my term as Postmaster General I have had ample opportunity to study these men and women at their work. I have made a practice of dropping in unexpectedly and at odd hours of the day and night. I have been in offices at midnight; I have been in offices at 6 a.m., and I have been in offices at just about every interval between those two times. I never failed to be impressed with the employees' cheerfulness, their capability and their determination to do their work swiftly and well. I have found in the postal service a quality of devotion and integrity that is, perhaps, unusual in this day of materialism and mass production.
I should like to commend the minister for those remarks, particularly his reference to the devotion to duty of postal employees, but with reference to the first part of his remarks I am wondering how they tie in with certain complaints I have received. Probably the minister can explain whether a matter of policy that is applied across the country is involved. The complaints brought to my attention have to do with the new post office and federal building nearing completion in the town of Timmins. Although I have not seen it yet, I have been given to understand that there is what I believe is called an observation gallery in the building.
I understand that the gallery is closed in with one-way glass. In other words, people can look out through this glass but people cannot look in. I understand that the purpose is for supervision of the employees and so on. I should like to ask hon. members whether they would feel completely at ease in their work if they realized that at any time big brother, the Postmaster General, might be looking over their shoulders. The employees who have brought this matter to my attention say that they have a sort of creepy feeling. They never know who is

watching them and when and they feel that their integrity is being questioned more than it should be. As I say, I do not know if this is a departmental policy and possibly the minister could give some explanation of the matter. Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak for only a minute or two. First of all, may I say that I think the minister is deserving of a compliment from myself as a member for a riding for which very little was done for a good number of years. Since my election in 1958 I along with other members from the area have been able to get the minister to consider plans for the establishment and erection of a new post office in the riding of Edmonton East. These facilities have been needed for a good many years and I wish to congratulate the minister on the way he has approached this problem and on the fact that the matter is finally in the planning stage.
The second problem I wish to bring to the minister's attention is one that has been brought to the attention of former ministers of the department by the east Edmonton businessmen's association. I refer to the need for facilities in the 118th avenue area. This is a section of the city of Edmonton where for some years business has been carried on in much the same way as in a small suburban town on the outskirts of a city.
There is suitable development in this area and the minister is aware of it as he visited this particular area with me last fall. I hope that serious consideration will be given to the establishment very soon of facilities in this area.
The second problem is one respecting a small town in the outskirts of my riding of Edmonton East, namely the town of Beverly. Ten years ago when this small town had a population of 2,500 people there were two postal facilities, namely two drug stores. The population of this area is now in excess of 10,000 people and they are being served by those two small drug stores some 40 blocks apart. I understand the minister is initiating an investigation into this particular area and service, and I hope that some good news will be forthcoming very soon in this regard.
I have only one other point to mention and this was brought to my attention by the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac. It is with respect to postage on overseas shipments to underprivileged countries and disaster areas. I am speaking specifically of shipments made by our welfare organizations which are obliged to pay the full postal rate

Supply-Post Office
on these shipments. I suggest that this is a burden on these organizations.

I do not intend unduly to delay the passage of item No. 1 of the estimates, Mr. Chairman. However, I believe the minister realizes that once we overcome the hurdle of item No. 1 there ought to be little delay in processing the remaining items under his department. I want to underline the point I made on May 27 which was not replied to at that time. I realize the minister was very optimistic and hoped that after a brief reply we might agree to the passage of item No. 1 at the time. I refer to my plea that the number necessary under the regulations for the institution of door to door delivery be greatly reduced. With all the unemployment we have in Canada at the present time and also with the changes in the living habits of the Canadian population, I feel that the old regulation calling for a minimum of 2,500 calls in any post office before door to door delivery is begun is in line for major consideration. I believe that half of that number ought to be adequate.
I know there are problems of hiring men and giving them the five-day week when giving delivery for six days a week is involved. However, according to my calculations, a community having 1,250 householders would require four men, with three men always on the go. To those four men we might even, under these conditions, be able to grant the eight-hour day and the five-day week.
I think that a new look might be taken at this problem. I would ask the minister whether some consideration will be given to this proposal. I think it might enable the department to pay a little more attention to municipal boundaries if this were done. In my riding it would enable the people of Port Moody to receive their mail via the Port Moody post office rather than, as is the case under present conditions, roughly one third of them having to get their mail out of the New Westminster post office in order to have the advantage of door to door delivery.
I should like to underline the pleas made in this chamber by the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Burn-aby-Richmond that growing and relatively new communities in major urban areas surrounding larger cities be supplied with separate post offices of their own. The minister's reply to the hon. member for New Westminster with regard to the Newton post office is found at page 4704 of Hansard. The minister had this to say:
I believe he also knows that we are looking at the question of a post office building for that area. However, we do not want to be drawn into the erection of a building on a specific location in an
[Mr. Skoreyko.l
area which is expanding and growing as rapidly as is that one until at least there is some firm indication as to the pattern of growth which is going to take place in the years ahead.
I recall that a number of years ago, if not as recently as one year ago, there was in the estimates an item for the building of a new post office in Newton. If the government knew as early as that time that a new post office was needed in that area or that municipality, and had obviously agreed that it was going to build one or that one ought to be built,
I must ask the minister in all sincerity whether that item was in the estimates at the time for political reasons only or whether there was any degree of sincerity toward obtaining a vote in this chamber for the supplying of the people of Newton with a post office. In particular, I should like him to explain why after the decision by the House of Commons to allow the building of a federal building at Newton there are apparently now no plans to proceed or even to use the money that was originally allowed.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond underlined the growing need for a post office in Burnaby in order to meet the requirements of the residents of Burnaby. I do not agree at all with his contention that there is only a small number of complaints as to the delivery of mail in Burnaby. In my experience the service rendered with regard to the delivery of mail has declined from year to year. It is my contention that the delivery of mail is going to decline in efficiency until at long last the government is going to grant us our own distribution arrangements.
I should also like the minister to explain what the present attitude of his department is with regard to the rental of post office buildings. I know the former minister of public works took a very firm position in this regard. It was his opinion, which was expressed in this house, that wherever possible the Department of Public Works ought to own the building and that there ought to be no arrangement whereby the department would grant a rental lease to an individual, who would then take that lease, go to the bank and obtain the loan necessary to finance entirely the cost of a building and who would be able to repay the whole of the cost of the building out of the rentals outlined in the lease, and then at the end of a five, seven or ten-year period he would remain the owner of the building toward the ownership of which he had supplied nothing except a little bit of organizational ability.
We have at this time a building in North Burnaby not owned by the department. We have a building in Port Moody not owned by the government and there is a building on the Kingsway not owned by the government. The

rental in at least one of these three cases is one of the highest rentals on a square footage basis that the Post Office Department is obligated to pay anywhere in the dominion. I would like to see the attitude of the government expressed as being identical with the attitude expressed a year or more ago, and I would like to see a little more action on the part of the government to implement this attitude, and that they either purchase existing buildings or erect their own buildings wherever it is economically right to do so, rather than renting buildings at exorbitant rates.
I should also like to make one additional reference to the reply of the minister to the representations of the hon. member for Vancouver East. The attitude of our group is that the taxpayers of Canada ought not to subsidize the distribution of advertising through the mails. I noted the minister's reply both on May 27 and again on June 8 when he emphasized that it is very important that there be the widest distribution of newspapers and magazines into the homes of the people of Canada.
I agree with that basic attitude of the minister. However, it is not the appearance and the distribution of the magazines and newspapers and other educational media that we take exception to; we feel that there is an undue amount of brain washing already in eixstence on the Canadian cultural scene and we do not like to see the post office being misused in order to enhance the interests of the advertisers of our nation.
The minister also said, as reported on page 4705 of Hansard for June 8:
-I see no necessity to ask the house to authorize any increase in the first-class postal rate.
May I assure the minister that neither the hon. member for Vancouver East nor any other member of our group advocated an increase in first-class postal rates at this or at any other time. However, we now adopt the attitude that the minister adopted when he was in opposition in 1954 when he advocated that the users of first-class mail be not penalized in order to make possible the distribution of the very heavy burden of advertising, which is indeed a heavy burden on our employees in the Post Office Department.
