Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity of bringing to the attention of the minister a problem which is of vital importance to the residents of one of our enterprising young communities in northern Manitoba. At the community of Snow Lake, Manitoba the people are receiving at the present time only tri-weekly mail service. This service has been going on for some time and up until very recently it was possibly the best service which could be provided by the Post Office Department because at that time there was only tri-weekly service on the trains travelling on the Hudson bay line from The Pas to Churchill. But now with further development at the new town-site of Thompson, Canadian National Railways have now inaugurated a daily service going northwards out of The Pas, and I would like the minister to give the very fullest consideration to investigating this situation to see if it would not be possible to take advantage of the new train service to give the people of Snow Lake a daily mail service.
In yesterday's mail I received a letter from the local administrator of that point. Attached to that letter was a very lengthy petition signed by the majority of the residents of Snow Lake. I understand that the original of this petition has been directed to the minister, and I sincerely request that this matter be given every consideration. I would like to point out that I am sure the people of Snow Lake would be very gratified to know that plans are under way for the construction of a new post office, and I certainly hope that this will be carried out as quickly as possible. The postmaster at Snow Lake has been performing very satisfactory service under sometimes adverse conditions due to lack of space in relation to the volume of mail which comes into this new community. This is a mining community, everyone there is employed, and I am quite sure I am safe in saying that there is a large volume of mail going in and out of Snow Lake.
There is one more small matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister concerning another point in northern Manitoba, Cranberry Portage. Some time ago complaints came in from the residents of Cranberry Portage in relation to the facilities of the post office at that point. As the result of these complaints an investigation took place and all of the complaints were fully investigated. One of the recommendations which came out of the investigation by the

Supply-Post Office
officials who made the investigation was that it was very desirable to have a post office at that point located in a separate self-contained building entirely apart from the building which it is now in, which also houses a general store. In January this recommendation went in and I was advised by the Post Office Department that they felt this should be done. I should like the minister to investigate this problem and, if possible, advise me as to just what progress has been made.
In closing I should like to commend the minister on the work he has been doing in operating the department and to thank him for the co-operation I have had in the past. I should also like to make a strong plea to him to see if improved mail services cannot be had for the people of Snow Lake. I do not believe it would be too difficult. Snow Lake is located about 36 miles off the Hudson bay line and has access by road to the railhead at Wekusko and trains arrive in We-kusko every day. It may need some new arrangement with the contractor who transports the mail from Wekusko to Snow Lake, but this mail contractor has some obligation to meet each train every day in other work which he performs and I do not think it would be too difficult to make arrangments for mail to be carried between Wekusko and Snow Lake.

I should like to ask the minister briefly about a matter in connection with curbside mail boxes. We have one in the riding which I represent which was put in on a trial basis. I believe there are others in other parts of Canada. I should like to have the minister tell us what success they have had with these curbside mail boxes where you can drive up in your car and put your mail in the box. It has been very popular in the city of St. Catharines and I understand there has been a request for a few more. The one we have was one of the first put in, but I think there could be some improvement in the design of the box itself. The one important factor is to make it weather-proof so that wind driven snow cannot get into the box. There are two types of curbside boxes. There is one with a conveyor belt that takes the mail into the post offices. I am not thinking of that. I am thinking of the boxes placed on residential streets where you can drive up in your car, put the mail in it and drive away.

I am reluctant to add an off note to what seems to be a happy afternoon with compliments flying and, I am sure, Compliments which are well deserved in some cases, but there is a matter which I feel is my duty to raise. Before doing so

I should like to take this opportunity to say that Canada is fortunate in having such a high calibre of civil servant across the country, and of that group none are more loyal or more devoted than those employed in the Post Office Department.
My question arises from two directives which were issued during 1959 in the Post Office Department and which seem to me to smell strongly of political meddling in the public service. It has to do with the functions of civil servants carrying out their normal duties and I think it adversely affects this important postal service to the Canadian people. Perhaps I could explain best and more briefly by citing an example of the appointment of a subpostmaster or the transfer and appointment of a subpostmaster.
With the development which has taken place in this country and around many of the large cities of this country I think this is becoming more and more of a problem as more and more of these offices are required to be opened. As I said, I think I can best explain by taking an instance where a subpostmaster resigns. Normally the procedure to be followed as I understand it would be for officials to explore the possibilities, to reexamine the area with a view to appointing a new subpostmaster. Now I understand that on the basis of a directive from Ottawa dated February 17, 1959 which dealt with the transfer and appointment of subpostmasters, and a further one of May 26, 1959 which dealt with the opening of subpost offices, postal officials from coast to coast have been affected, and as a result of those directives they are unable to take the necessary action to maintain this service. On the contrary they must wait for instructions, and any applications, I understand, that are received locally, and this applies to all Canada, must be forwarded to Ottawa for approval, which seems to me can only mean political approval.
That is a backward step. It is a step which I think interferes with the normal functions of officials of the Post Office Department. That sort of thing may have been good enough back in the old horse and buggy days but I do not think it is good enough for 1960 and I would ask the Postmaster General if he will give serious consideration to rescinding these two directives, the one of February 17 dealing with the transfer and appointment of subpostmasters and the one of May 26 dealing with the opening of subpost offices. I ask him if he will consider rescinding these directives which I believe are politically inspired.

I should like to make a few brief remarks on the subject of the postal service through Nelson and points east and point out, first of all, that at the present time

there is a very close connection with the postal service at Nelson. I understand that one truck brings the mail into Nelson and the other leaves almost immediately, so that if the Vancouver mail truck is late getting in the mail is held up indefinitely until a connection can be made. I would suggest that more leeway be allowed in connecting truck times between Nelson and points east.
Another point I wish to raise concerns registered mail services. I do not think we are providing the service that we should provide to many of the rural communities. I had an instance brought to my attention where a letter was registered at a point in the lake Windermere valley to another point eight miles away. In view of the regulations which require, apparently, that the letter has to go to a subpost office, by the time it had gone around it was 10 days before the letter was finally received although there was only such a short distance involved. So I would like to suggest that a small bag or pouch be utilized for this purpose so that registered mail could be handled without this serious delay.
Another point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister concerns airmail service. I feel that in many of these smaller communities especially in our area when first-class mail is picked up it should be immediately transferred to a point where it will connect with air mail service. It should be forwarded by air mail from the distribution point rather than being transported by truck as it is at the present time.
I should like to cite an example of what I mean. If a letter is mailed in Creston in time to catch the mail truck out of Creston at ten o'clock in the morning the letter is taken to Cranbrook. It travels by truck until it reaches Calgary the following day. It is late getting into Calgary and it is not delivered in Calgary until the following morning. If that first-class mail out of Creston were transferred at the post office in Cranbrook to the air mail service it would be in Calgary within four hours after mailing in Creston.
This is something to which we should give consideration. We are giving air mail service to the larger centres and I feel similar services could be provided to smaller communities rather than allowing first-class mail to take the usual course of delivery.
Apart from these suggestions I have made we are very well satisfied with the rules and regulations of the Post Office Department. I believe that the Postmaster General is turning out sound regulations and that he and his staff are doing an excellent job of mail delivery under conditions that are often difficult in our part of the country,
Supply-Post Office
particularly in the winter months. I would be grateful if the two or three matters I have mentioned could be given consideration. I do not feel it is asking too much to have given to people in rural areas the postal service that is given to people in larger centres.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Post Office Department is one of the most highly socialized operations in the world today. We want it to be as efficient as possible because it proves something we want proved not only here but throughout the world.
We will keep the hon. member away from it then.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Canada has done a good job in supplying mail service at a reasonable price and the results are highly satisfactory. The salaries of postal employees come under the Civil Service Act and do not come within the purview of the minister. The Postmaster General should pay closer attention to the wages and working conditions in post offices than he has in the past.
The minister spoke of his visits to post offices throughout Canada and stated that he arrived at all hours of the day and night. When I worked in the mines we sometimes had bosses drop in unexpectedly. Mines are dark, dismal and not well lighted and sometimes we would take a long lunch hour. We never appreciated unexpected visits from our boss under those circumstances. I draw this to the minister's attention.
I suggest that if we raised the salaries of postal employees we would not have to have snooper systems or runways and pilfering would be reduced. I appreciate that runways are not only a technological advance but serve as a check on employees. The days are gone when supervision of this kind is required. We should improve salary standards and working conditions.
Progress has been made in terms of promotions within the department but the progress is not fast enough to suit me. I recently travelled on a train with a friend with whom I had worked in a mine. He is an honest and conscientious employee. He accepted a job in the Post Office Department in Ottawa two or three years ago and although the wages were adequate and the working conditions not unpleasant he has already grown dissatisfied with the lack of opportunities for promotion or advancement. I have heard this from other employees of post offices including the one at Kirkland Lake of which I have knowledge. Promotions are not always accorded under civil service regulations on the basis of seniority or in accordance with skill or acquired knowledge. Often someone

Supply-Post Office
is brought in from outside which precludes opportunities for advancement among the local employees.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman would permit me to make a statement at this point. If the hon. member will look in the official gallery he will see the deputy minister who started off his career as a clerk in the department. He will see another official, just below the deputy minister in rank, who began his career as a letter carrier. He will also observe another couple of fellows in the official gallery who started off slugging mail bags somewhere in the back of a post office. If the hon. gentleman would direct his attention to the table of the house I believe he would see another man who started off in the Post Office Department as well. I believe that is a pretty good answer to there being inadequate opportunities for advancement within the department. The answer can be found in the gentlemen sitting up in the official gallery.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am amazed and gratified by that information. My hon. friend described the situation as he sees it. It may be that promotions are slow through no fault of the system but through a failure of the departmental officials to disseminate information about opportunities for advancement among employees of the department.
There are a number of other problems that 1 should like to discuss. Some of them affect the wage structure of the postal employees for the work they do. I have had complaints in my riding from people getting $270 a month on which they have to keep a family. They are doing a job which involves walking up to 14 miles a day carrying heavy mail bags. They have responsibility for confidential matters and for financial documents. They have responsibility that is considerably above that which would be given to an individual in any other industry at that rate of pay. I think they have grounds for complaint.
In many instances they object to the fact that they cannot use their own cars for transporting their mail sacks from the general post office to where they are going to deliver their mail. Most of them have cars and they would like to throw the bag in the back seat and drive 20 or 30 blocks and then pick up their route from there and leave the car parked on a side street and pick it up again after they are through. They tell me they are not allowed to do this. This may be true of only one or two post offices, but it is true in one. They object to this; they think they should be allowed to use their cars. There may be very good reasons why they are not allowed to use them, but in the

smaller communities they could use the same system that is used in the suburbs of large cities where they have pick-up depots. The mail is taken to those depots and the mail man, instead of going to the main post office gets his mail from this particular depot. This may be an answer in part to the problem.
We have another problem that affects my riding because it is an urban and rural riding. I refer to the matter of rural mail delivery. The minister may say that this is not general, and I will agree. It is not even general in my riding, but it happens to be general in this particular area. We have asked for a survey to be made to see whether something can be done to solve this particular problem. I understand the department is working on it. I received this letter which will explain the problem fairly well:
As you probably know, this rural route is operated from Charlton some seven miles west of Englehart. At present we enjoy thrice weekly delivery and pick-up, i.e., Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays. There is an R.R. 2 also serviced from Charlton which only gets twice weekly delivery.
Though only having three deliveries a week is bad enough, yet the length of time taken for mail to reach us from outside points, and the time for mail picked up here to get to its destination is absolutely unbelievable.
For instance, a letter requiring an immediate reply is received here on a Thursday. The reply is picked up on the Saturday. It does not leave Charlton until the following Monday and its arrival, say, in Toronto is on Tuesday and delivery there may not be till Wednesday. Mail for Kirkland Lake some 25 miles away has to be placed on the train, taken to North Bay then after sorting brought back by train to Swastika thence to Kirkland.
Incoming mail is just as bad. It takes papers (and letters) just as long to reach us from Kirkland as from Toronto.
Toronto is 400 miles away. I continue:
Papers published in Kirkland on Friday are not delivered here till the next Tuesday, the Toronto papers for the same day also arriving at the same time.
Letters from Tarzwell, only a few miles north of here are first taken to Swastika, thence to North Bay, then back to Englehart, then to Charlton and finally, days later, arrive at their addressees.
He goes on to say it is useless to complain to the officials and this is the part I should like to read:
Just one additional delivery through the week, on Monday, would mean an awful lot to us, and, if such could be effected I would certainly see that you are given the credit for bringing this about.
He wrote me another letter subsequent to this and this is what he said in part:
I have another glaring example of the inefficient, inadequate mail service in this locality.
At 10.03 p.m. on March 18 a telegram was handed in to Canadian National Telegraphs in Toronto. It was received in Englehart the same night. As we, in this modern community have no phones, the wire was mailed to me on Saturday, March 19. I received it at 11 a.m. Tuesday March 22.

Luckily, the telegram only announced the birth of a grand-daughter, but the whole point is that it would have been the same had the wire carried the news of a death or a fatal illness. And, of course, it could happen to anyone living on these ill-served mail routes.
In this connection it is interesting to note that the ''Telegram"-
This is the Telegram newspaper.
-of Saturday, March 19 carried the birth announcement. It arrived at the same time as the telegram which was sent some 24 hours earlier. And we in Canada are so far ahead of other nations in our ways of life, or are we?
All I want to do is to point out that we have problems and some of these problems concern our rural delivery routes. We have not kept up to date on those routes as we have in the urban areas. In my opinion we have the opportunity now of combining many of the rural routes, particularly in my area. I cannot speak for other areas but I think that conditions there are much about the same. The rural routes were laid out when we were driving horses, when the mail, certainly in the wintertime, had to be delivered by horse-drawn conveyances and the routes had to be kept to certain limits. Now automobiles are used in the summer time and in the main the routes are all snowplowed in the winter time. It would be a very simple matter in some instances to combine two and in other instances more than two rural delivery routes so that mail could be delivered much faster and much more effectively than it is at the present time.
On a number of occasions I have asked for changes in these mail routes. The method of proceeding is to take out a petition. When a petition is taken out it makes a lot of people angry because it means changing from a rural post office to rural delivery. After the petition is taken out, and overwhelmingly those petitions are in favour of one type of service or the other, nothing happens. In some cases this action is repeated two or three times over a period of four or five years with the same result.

The
hon. member refers to some cases. Will he give me two or three examples?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am thinking of one in particular, namely Uno Park. The second one is Thornloe. I have been involved in the one at Uno Park on two occasions. I do not know what the result is of the last request of two or three months ago but I do know that a gentleman who took out the petition, who had raised the matter with me the first time, tells me that none of his close neighbours will talk to him any more because they
Supply-Post Office
wanted the post office instead of the rural delivery, and yet the petition was quite highly supported.
This type of thing does not make for good relations in the community when it is done on this basis. The situation is changing. Conditions must have been laid down in the first place for establishing the set-up that was established. Conditions change all the time. I am thinking of road clearance and snow removal in the wintertime. Conditions are vastly changed from what they were. This means that the service can be changed and in many instances better service can be given.
We have another problem that I am concerned with which is in the transitional stage now. To date it has not produced any bad results in my area but I think it can and will, and also in Cochrane north. I refer to the sorting of mail on trains. There used to be mail cars on all O.N.R. trains but now sorting is done only on some of them. It meant that when the post office closed at six o'clock, or at whatever time it might close, people who wanted to get mail on the train would go to the station and drop their mail in the appropriate box, depending on whether the letter was to go north or south, and the mail would be delivered the next morning. The service from Ottawa or Toronto to northern Ontario is very fast provided certain conditions are met. If I mail a letter at four o'clock this afternoon and it leaves our subpost office and goes to the station directly rather than going through the main post office it will be delivered in Kirkland Lake tomorrow afternoon. If it goes through the local post office it may be a matter of many days. If it happens to be a brown envelope it will sometimes take four or five days, but normally first-class mail will be delivered immediately.
This situation is repeated all along the line, and one reason that return mail service has been so satisfactory is that the mail is sorted on the train by the postal staff. Even in the case of mail addressed to a small community ten miles away from the point of mailing, the postal staff are able to operate speedily enough to be able to drop this mail off at its destination although it may only be a few miles away. Service to these communities takes one day or less.
I am told that a number of postal employees have been taken off the northern run, that the sorting is only done at the centres now and that the mail is transported by truck. As a result, there is no service available to many of the small communities as was the case before. If mail is left at the post office after hours it remains there until

Supply-Post Office
the next day because obviously there is nobody there to sort it. The truck driver can only handle sorted mail and mail cannot be given to the truck driver to take to its destination until it is sorted because he is hired on the basis of conveying mail and not to handle or deal with it in any other way. There would be no cancellation of the stamps if the truck driver were to take such mail and I understand he is instructed not to do so, which I think is quite right.
We in northern Ontario would like more consideration to be given to this matter before any further curtailment in the sorting of mail on mail cars takes place. It may be that reconsideration can be given to those areas where this practice has been discontinued because it was serving a very useful purpose and providing a service that we need badly. We are a long distance from the main centres and a great deal of our business is done by mail. Telegrams are even more difficult to deliver to many of the small communities. Our mail service has been very satisfactory and we would like to see it kept on as high a level of efficiency as possible.
I have seen the situation that has developed in other areas of Ontario and which may develop in our area. I can remember being in southwestern Ontario a few years ago and a letter from Toronto to Dundalk, Orangeville or Collingwood took five days to get to its destination. I know that because my cheque used to be sent to me by mail and I would go to the post office every day for five or six days before I got my cheque. I hope that the minister, in giving consideration to the better distribution of mail to small communities, will take this matter into account. I have talked to people in the area I have mentioned and the mail service there is no better now than it was when I was there.
I suggest that the same thing could happen in northern Ontario and I say there is no reason why it should. We have been very satisfied with the mail service we have had and we would like to continue to receive that type of service. Therefore I ask the minister to give very careful consideration to the matter of changing from the sorting of mail on the train and using a truck distribution service instead. In the limited areas where the new service has been used or where it has not been possible to give service by rail because of the discontinuation of rail service to communities such as Matachewan the results have not been very satisfactory. When the railway went into that area the postal service was much better than it is now with the present system of transportation by truck and bus.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to say very much on this item but I cannot help adding some words in praise of the Post Office Department. I think it should be said that the administrative staff of the department is excellent. As Canadians we should be proud of our post office system. I do not take anything away, of course, from the hard working minister because in working hard and giving attention to his department I think he rates as high as anyone who has occupied that office in the past. My heart does not bleed too much for the situation of the administrative staff generally. I think their conditions of work are good and their salaries are fairly well rated at the present time.
But I am always interested in learning more about the mail sorters and the men who deliver the mail. I should like the minister to bring me up to date as to their situation. I have always thought that these men are entitled to special consideration. Although they are not professionals as far as education is concerned, they are professionals having regard to the service they give. They make our lives a little more cheerful when we go to the door to receive our mail. I do not know whether they are trained that way, but I like to see the postman come to my door. In spite of any trouble he may have in his home life, he always seems to forget that, always inquires about me and tries to find out if he can be helpful. For that alone I think they should receive special consideration with respect to their remuneration.
There is one situation that always worries me. These men toil under rather heavy loads that we would not like to have to carry every day. There has been some improvement in this regard in recent years, but there still must be some men who after five, ten or fifteen years become physically not as able to do the job and cannot carry on. This applies also to some sorters whose work involves the use of their eyes and physical effort. I should like to know what happens to these men if after a period of time they cannot carry on their work. Are they placed in positions in other sections of the department at equal remuneration or do many have to leave their employment altogether? It is my impression that there are not many who lose their positions on account of the fact that they cannot carry on the work they have been doing. I hope the minister will be able to answer this question and at the same time I hope he will be able to tell the committee that he appreciates as much as any other member that the sorters and the men who carry our mail are entitled to special consideration in their rates of pay. I hope he will

lead the fight at all times, as he should, to see that the civil service commission realizes that our letter carriers are not just people who are walking the streets and throwing letters in mail boxes but are professionals in their field. I think all members of the house will agree with me on that.

Mr. Chairman, I want to assure the minister that I am not rising with anything but good will for him and for the department. Over the years I have found that the department takes into consideration in a very friendly spirit representations made to it by members of parliament, no matter what their political persuasion may be. I have always been pleased, as I say, with the investigations that have been taking place as a result of inquiries I have made or suggestions I have advanced to the Post Office Department. If I have any criticism at all, it is not of the personnel in the head office or in the district offices; it is rather I think of a system that has developed, shall I say.
While they respond with the utmost consideration to suggestions that have come from me as to improvements in services, over the years I have developed the feeling that somehow, perhaps under pressure from treasury board, there has been an extra consciousness of the budget and a fear of adding anything different or new to the budget. Sometimes they find it necessary to do something after a community or after a member of parliament makes a request. I sometimes think they should perhaps initiate some of these things themselves much more quickly when conditions change.
A great number of trains have been taken off. I sometimes think that the staff itself has not been too quick to adopt alternatives to replace perhaps a daily service to which we were accustomed to; and, for instance, when local trains are no longer in existence, to substitute transportation by truck or otherwise. Too often they seem to wait for a nudge from the community or from the member of parliament. I think the difficulty does not lie in the fact that they do not see these things. Rather I think the difficulty lies in the fact that they have had such a great amount of pressure upon them as to the need of not increasing their expenses that we sometimes find it necessary to make suggestions more often than we seem to be obliged to in connection with some other departments.
I do not want to repeat some of the excellent suggestions that have been made today, last Wednesday and on a previous occasion when the minister was before us with the administration item. I think perhaps 79951-0-315
Supply-Post Office
I might be introducing something that has not been discussed so far. I want to draw the attention of the minister and his officials to the fact that in some of the northern areas of our country where the population might be predominantly Indian we have in recent years been experiencing a change in the life that is being led there. Instead of sending many of the youngsters out to residential schools there has been a trend to establish day schools. Instead of sending the people out to hospitals and to doctors there has developed a pattern of small nursing stations through the community. I think the minister will be well acquainted with the fact that the economics branch of Indian affairs is attempting to have projects for timber resources development and the development of fisheries in the lakes in order to guide them to try to develop these activities. In consequence, their existence to a great extent is not the nomadic, moving-around type of existence as they have had in the past. We have now in many places- and certainly this situation applies in the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River-greater permanency in the life that is being led there. In consequence, air services are improved. The local services are on a regular basis rather than on a charter basis in many instances I could indicate to the department. Inasmuch as this regular schedule service is available at several of the headquarters of our bands I feel that a careful look should be given to the desirability of establishing the normal postal services that would be provided to that number of people if they were situated in any other part of the country. There is greater permanency now. The nomadic life is not being led. I think there is justification for setting up postal services.
There are one or two other items upon which the minister would perhaps care to comment either now or when we meet the appropriate item in his estimates. We are all aware that the annual report that is publicly available refers to the year ending something more than a year ago. Perhaps the minister might give us an indication of what has happened in the meantime with respect to commemorative stamps and perhaps he might give us an outline of what his schedule is with respect to new stamps for the present fiscal year.
In the annual report of the department for the year ended March 31, 1959 I note that the minister indicated the numbers of post office savings banks that are provided. Can he break that figure down as to the number of points in which there are postal savings banks but in which there would not be a branch of one of our chartered banks.

Supply-Post Office
I have had some experience with the benefits that have developed from the easing of regulations which are referred to on page 11 of the same report. The wording of the report is as follows:
-the regulations restricting letter carrier delivery across vacant land have been eased.
I wonder whether it would not be appropriate for us to have on Hansard, from the experience gained, a short description of the effects of these new regulations. I certainly know that in one of the larger communities of my area this easing has proved helpful because, by reason of the terrain in our part of northern Ontario where we have a great deal of water and a number of rocks, we have settlements established in fingers of the area which are sometimes quite a distance from the centre of the community.
Reference was made the other day, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Port Arthur, to the possibility of establishing group boxes in some of our communities where settlement is now some distance from the one and only post office in the community. In both instances I think he was referring to communities which have not a population that would under present regulations, justify the establishment of a letter carrier delivery system. In his reply last Wednesday the minister did not completely give me the information that I perhaps would be seeking, namely whether or not delivery by means of group boxes can be provided even in communities where letter carrier delivery service has not been established.
The other item with regard to which I would appreciate having some information on record because there is a great deal of interest in the matter is what the progress has been in the minimum numbers of householders that have been required over the years before the Post Office Department would entertain a request for letter carrier service. I think the number is now 2,500. But as I recall it, the last time in my constituency that we were able to persuade the department to institute a new letter carrier service the figure prevailing then was either 1,600 or 1,800. I was just wondering when the 2,500 unit figure was established.
In the debate and in the departmental report reference has been made to marine services. Does the postal transportation department provide marine mail service except by utilizing some already existing water carrier that is operating on a schedule similar to the arrangements that have been provided historically by the railway? If not, in what circumstances does the department enter into the establishment of new contracts with carriers perhaps carrying only mail?

I am not going to repeat at any length the feelings that have been expressed by hon. members on all sides of the chamber that the services provided by our letter carriers and some of our more humble clerks and sorters in the offices do not, under present conditions, seem to be remunerated on a scale that to many of us seems to be comparable and fair with respect to other occupations, both those in the non-government service in our highly organized union communities and indeed in some of the other departments.
I gave a specific illustration to the minister which rather continues to arouse my concern. I think in a community like Rainy River the postmaster has responsibilities, but without detailed information of the functions of that post and the funcitons of non-managerial numbers of the staff of the customs or immigration branch, I do not think his responsibilities are comparable with that of a routine member of the staff at the border point who would inspect visitors. I think that is an example and perhaps the post office has not been able to be as persuasive in the matter of increased salaries for some of its personnel as have some other departments. I think the difference in salary between those two posts is about $1,500. In my view there is no comparison between the attitude taken by the members of the community as to the responsibility of the postmaster himself and one who is not the senior man in either the department of customs or the department of immigration, one who is simply doing border checking at that point without the responsibilities of management.

Mr. Chairman, I have in my riding an association called the superannuated civil servants. I have had several meetings with their executive in regard to a problem which is not properly a problem of the Postmaster General but which I should like to draw to his attention and ask his good offices to try to further the aims of this group.
A prime problem in a large city is that of casual help at Christmastime and the postmaster likes to get experienced personnel to act as straw bosses, so to speak, foremen, over help which has had no previous post office experience. But according to the act which governs superannuation and pensions, these men cannot earn in any one month more than they earned at the time they left the service. This is a very fair regulation and a very right and proper one. However, I think its application to casual help could bear a little looking into because I know of one case where a man in the city of Vancouver worked through at the request of the postmaster and his pay had to be adjusted to 65 cents an

hour because it simply went over the amount he was allowed to earn. In other cases they have to make a refund.
I have had letters on this and I have seen the letters which deal with it. The department has acted according to the letter of the law, but I would like the Postmaster General, if he would, to confer with his colleague the Minister of Finance and see whether some arrangement can be made whereby casual help who are only employed for a few weeks or a month might be exempted from these regulations.

Mr. Chairman, I shall only take a moment of the minister's time but I want to draw to his attention one or two difficulties we are having at Sudbury, particularly since the amalgamation which took place on January 1 of this year.
In this amalgamated area naturally the four cents local postage rate will apply, with the exception of one area. I have had a great amount of correspondence complaining about people who receive their mail at this particular post office, which is not a sub, where letters have been mailed to them carrying a four cents stamp but when they go to pick up their mail they are charged two cents extra for this service.
I might say that this area is much closer to the city than some of the annexed areas which are already, and have been for some time, enjoying carrier service, with the exception of the one area about which I am speaking. I know that this post office was recently renovated by the Post Office Department and I would presume that a lease of some length has been taken on this building. However, I suggest that when this lease is over this post office be removed and the area that it serves can then in many cases apply for carrier service which is enjoyed by other areas much further removed from the central post office in the city, areas such as Minnow Lake, Gatchell, New Sudbury and part of Lockerby, the community of which I am speaking. All these areas are already enjoying letter carrier service, but the area around this post office is not.
At the same time there are two areas adjacent to it on either side which would like to qualify for rural route delivery and have community boxes established, but due to the location of the post office I am led to believe that rural route service cannot apply within half a mile of either side of a recognized post office. If such is the case I hope it will be looked into and that service can be given to these two areas in the form of a rural route service, which they will be 79951-0-315J
Supply-Post Office
pleased to get instead of having to travel the great distance to this post office. I know that many of the people living in these areas are having their mail delivered to their business addresses in the city rather than trying to pick it up at the Lockerby post office.
The particular beef I have, of course, is the four cents stamp and the two cents additional at this one post office, but nowhere else in the amalgamated area. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, may I call the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) to a stamp that was sent to me recently, from a source I cannot reveal.
At first sight, I thought it was a prehistoric animal, but using a magnifying glass, I was able to read the name of the Hon. Wilfrid Labbe, a member of the Union Na-tionale and of Mr. Barrette's cabinet.
May I also suggest to the minister that there should be a rule against affixing such stamps to letters. The one I have here gives the impression of being a current issue, and I really do not think we should tolerate the use of such stamps on correspondence that is sent and delivered through the Post Office Department.
We owe it to ourselves to allow all charitable organizations to use promotion stamps, but surely not stamps such as the one I received, which incidentally was quite unattractive. Besides, in my estimation envelopes are no place for such stamps.
I therefore ask the minister to inquire as to whether stamps of this type, used purely for election purposes-because such stamps are misleadingly similar to regular stamps-might have been cancelled in post offices, thus causing the government to lose revenue.
I leave the matter with the minister, and I am sending the stamp over to him so that he may have a look at it. However, I would ask him to return it, because after June 22, such stamps will become rarities, indeed, and I would like to hang on to that one. (Text):

Mr. Chairman, I would like to clear up one or two small points which I made in my previous remarks when I was talking about the scope of the football pools in Britain. Apparently I understated the number of pools and the amount of business they did. I was really only referring to one pool, and while it is the largest of the pool organizations it is only one of eight comparable organizations.

For example, the equivalent to our Minister of Finance in Great Britain also has a type of legalized gamble going, in that people who buy certain types of bonds and savings certificates over there have what amounts to an opportunity to win big prizes.

speechtext: Order. I might just point out that when the hon. member discussed this the other day the Postmaster General referred to the fact that this came under the Criminal Code. I do not think, therefore, that the hon. gentleman can continue along that line.

I imagined it was affected by the operations of the Post Office Department, but I could be mistaken. Anyway I have had some mail since making my remarks which indicates that there are a substantial number of people desperately trying to play the football pools who are fed up with the attempts of the Postmaster General to block their efforts.
I turn now to something which I know is the responsibility of the minister. This is something which the hon. member for Vancouver East brought up. He compared the attitude of the minister toward the loss in carrying newspapers and periodicals in the old days with his actions now. One of the points in which I would be interested is the relationship in the loss, which I understand to be about $26 million-I say "loss" but I really mean loss of revenue, because that is what it is, rather than an actual loss-between the carrying of a large number of United States periodicals which now come to our country and the Canadian periodicals and newspapers. Could the minister give us a breakdown? These are newspapers as against periodicals, although I know that technically a newspaper is a periodical. There are only 100 daily newspapers in Canada at the moment and there are not too many weeklies. I wonder if the minister would have any kind of a break-down so that we could analyse this $26 million loss in revenue to see if it would not be possible to kill two birds with one stone, that is, to get more revenue and to give Canadian periodicals an advantage as compared with the United States magazines which come in and not only take away circulation but advertising revenue.
I know this could be looked upon as an extra tax, and there may be difficulties about dealing with magazines coming in from another country. I get magazines sent to me very week from Britain and it always seems fantastic that a big bundle of magazines can come in all the way from London for a one

and a half penny stamp. Maybe there has been some international agreement worked out, but if it is a fact we are losing so much revenue, and if a substantial proportion of it is the result of carrying United States and other foreign periodicals, we might consider some agreement to raise the price to the post office for carrying it.
One of the ironies about the newspaper situation in Canada today is a political one.
1	do not know of a newspaper in Canada that claims to be anything other than a spokesman of free enterprise. I am thinking especially of a Thompson paper or a paper such as the Globe and Mail which I understand has the largest circulation of any newspaper in Canada. These newspapers are preeminently for private enterprise and it always puzzled me to think that there might be this inconsistency about free enterprise. There is, of course, the fact that these free enterprises allow their employees in Ottawa to exist in government rooms at government expense down the third floor corridor, for example. But here is a bigger and more costly thing. We have these free enterprisers being, in effect, subsidized by the public purse if this loss of $26 million represents substantially the fact that the post office is carrying Canadian newspapers and periodicals. For that reason I should like to get a closer idea of the relative amount. I would like to know how much subsidy we are giving to these free enterprisers to publish free enterprise Canadian newspapers.
Take the Globe and Mail, for example, which takes delight in pointing out all the subsidies on western wheat and all the subsidies paid to farmers in general. These papers continually preach the gospel of free enterprise, rugged individualism, standing on your own two feet and so on, yet this is a paper which I understand has the largest mailed circulation of any daily newspaper in Canada and as a consequence this free enterprise operation is in receipt of substantial assistance from the government.
There is another aspect of this question which I suppose the minister has already considered. That is the question of the reason for this subsidy. If the minister looks at volume

These publishers right after confederation, came to Ottawa every time it appeared that parliament was trying to get the post office to raise the charges on this particular kind of mail and their argument always was that they performed a primary role in educating the Canadian people. I think this argument probably had much greater substance in the nineteenth century than it has today when educational advantages are so much more evident and when people can turn to the schools, to books, to public libraries and to radio and television services. So it seems to me that this particular argument in favour of this kind of subsidy no longer stands.
The argument used to be that to many people on back farms and in distant parts of Canada the newspapers were the only means of providing cheap information. It does not seem to me that this argument stands up any longer, so I think we should ask these free enterprisers to be free enterprisers and stop leaning on the Canadian government in this regard.
The last point I wish to make relates to post office employees. I think every member of parliament has had conversations with the postal carriers, and I think it is generally agreed that this particular group, as a result of the rationalization of the department which bespeaks efficiency, works rather hard. It is my general impression that it is almost impossible for them to have a soft touch.
In terms of requests for increased wages they are not in the bargaining position that trade unionists are. Two things are pointed out to them in reply to their arguments for higher pay. They are often told that there is a waiting list of people who want to become letter carriers. There is no market demand competing for their services as there is in the case of dentists or people in other
Supply-Post Office
occupations. The other factor is that the services they render to the post office are of little use beyond the postal service. In other words, it is almost impossible for a letter carrier to work for three of four years and then value that service in the labour market at a high level because it is not sufficiently specialized to make him much more useful an employee than someone who enters the labour market for the first time.
According to postal employees with whom I have spoken the factors I have outlined render it difficult for them to present a case. There is no competition in the labour market for their services and there is no increment in their earning value when they are working for the department. This is becoming more and more the fate of many people in the kind of employment situation we are building up today with large organizations in which there is no particular specialization. I hope the minister will realize that these are factors that the employees have little chance to change.
Another related factor is that the income level at which these men happen to be is not a very high one. Indeed, it seems to me that it is one of the lowest in the civil service just in terms of the physical exertion and mental alertness that are required. That kind of physical exertion and mental alertness has no parallel value in the market place and yet it seems to me it should be recognized by putting it on a higher base of pay. I hope the minister is pressing his colleagues and especially the Minister of Finance who is the important minister in this area with all the energy and persuasion at his command to see that this group of employees gets an increase in pay and I hope a substantially higher minimum. By that I mean between $300 and $700, somewhere in that range. If we could return to our constituencies with the good news already abroad I know it would make it pleasanter for members of parliament.
I may be out of order in raising the following point because it relates to privileges of members of parliament. Has the minister had any discussion with anyone about the question of the parliamentary frank that we have as members? Has there been any thought of extending it for a longer period? No one would want to see hon. members using the frank on a year-round basis for the purpose of mailing out party propaganda and circulars and so on. I know that other hon. members I have talked to have a problem similar to mine and especially those hon. members from Quebec and the maritimes. The parliamentary frank is a great convenience. There is more than the question of the cost of stamps involved. It would be a great convenience if

Supply-Post Office
we could have franking privileges both in Ottawa and in our constituencies for most of the year. With the sessions becoming so lengthy and with the regular follow-up that is required on much of the correspondence one has, the purchase of postage stamps is a substantial financial whack. In addition there is the added annoying inconvenience of going out to purchase the stamps, sticking them on, and so on, the cost of which has to be met by a group of people who do not have great resources.
Has the minister the power of initiating any discussion along these lines or, as a member of parliament, would the minister consider taking up the suggestion and seeing what the people who have the power and initiative may think or feel about it?
Will the minister reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will try to be as brief as possible at this point. Some of the questions raised have been answered and I shall attempt to deal with some of the other matters in general terms. As hon. members have perhaps come to know, when there are certain points which require so much detail that they cannot be dealt with successfully and succinctly here in the committee it has been our practice to write the hon. member concerned immediately following the debate giving him the information requested.
As I have stated, some of the points raised come up year after year. I have come to the conclusion that this is almost automatic in the post office service. I wish to make the following brief excursion because I think it is interesting. I was interested to learn that what we thought was a new and modern process, the idea of photographing letters on reduced strips of film and sending the filmstrips by air mail, goes back not only through the wars but through peacetime to the Franco-German war of 1871 when the French post office successfully worked out such a system.
According to "An Outline of Postal History and Practice", a most interesting book, the French post office photographed letters at that time on to thin films of collodion. As the book states:
The films were rolled up tightly and placed In a small quill, which was attached to one of the tail feathers of the bird.
The bird was a carrier pigeon which served as the basis of the air mail delivery of those letters. Several hundreds of thousands of letters at that time were sent in this fashion between the United Kingdom and France almost 100 years ago. I believe this illustrates my point that the same kind of questions do crop up from time to time here in the committee.

A number of hon. members dealt with the question of salaries. I know that they know that this is basically a matter for the Minister of Finance. I think they also realize that it is one that is receiving sympathetic consideration at the present time and that I am personally very much aware both of their views and of those of the post office employees.
When speaking of the employees of the department 1 should on their behalf express the thanks of every one of them for the kind things which have been said about them here today. The hon. member for St. Denis earlier on took issue with me for having reported to the committee the accomplishments of the Post Office Department. I make no apology for doing so but I am very much aware, as I also pointed out at that time, that our success is based not only on the efforts of any one individual but on the tremendous efforts of a vast group of people.
The second thing that appeared to arouse the interest and curiosity of many hon. members was the use of the phrase "personal and confidential" on a fair amount of my correspondence. I was actually happy to find that this was referred to by approximately 12 hon. members many of whom made special speeches on this subject because when we reach the point at which the use of the phrase "personal and confidential" on a letter which goes to a member of parliament is the subject for debate in the consideration of the estimates of this department we have certainly reached a point at which there is apparently not too much in the department itself and its administration to be criticized. In reaching that point hon. members are, as it were, scraping the very bottom of the barrel.
Actually the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville gave us an example illustrating one of the principal reasons why this phrase is used on my correspondence when he said a letter sent to him had not been opened until he could open it himself and this caused him to miss an invitation which I had sent to him. I regret the fact that he missed the invitation, but members of parliament are writing me constantly on various matters, many of which are of interest only to themselves, many of which as far as I know they do not want bruited around too widely. As a result, I have tried, by marking these letters in this way, to ensure that the information goes directly to the member of parliament and is used by him as he sees fit. In many instances members have come to me and said, "I have this letter; have you any objection to the information being used?" And invariably, or almost invariably, I have said, "Absolutely not". But at least this does

respect a member of parliament and insures the fact that the information goes directly to him.
Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, I remember getting a letter on one occasion from the hon. member for Essex East when he was a minister. It brought birthday greetings and it was marked "personal". I think probably the same sort of thing applied at that time.
Individual problems such as those of the hon. member for Skeena, as I have said, we will deal with and report on. Since he spoke this morning I have been able to get some information. In so far as the service at this community of Nass river is concerned, we are attempting to improve its quality. We have got a contractor all ready to do it along the route, but now we have to cross the river and at the moment we are looking for somebody who will contract a boat service across the river at Greenville because the route is on the far side, as he knows. We hope to be successful in that respect.
The hon. member mentioned the letter carrier service in Kitimat. As he knows so well, our requirement is 2,500 houses. The present number is substantially under that; it is at the 2,000 mark, that is actually occupied houses, at the moment, and as soon as it reaches the 2,500 mark we will be delighted to institute the service there because other considerations such as weather are not going to stop the post office; I assure him of that.
The hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska made a number of interesting points. In the case of Dalhousie, we look forward to introducing letter carrier service there but it has not reached our requirements. I can assure him there is no shortage of rural mail boxes, nor are we overlooking areas where it is possible to give rural mail service.
The hon. member for Kootenay West said that his major criticism was with regard to the use of "personal and confidential" on letters and then he went on and spoke for 20 minutes on other matters so that his criticism in that respect must have been very forceful indeed. He asked us to keep post office lists more exact in so far as occupations are concerned. We do our best in that respect. Having indicated he likes to use the lists, he then criticized us for having them or, rather, he suggested someone else had criticized us for having them; that that information was information which should not be made available. Actually these lists are basically similar to those that one will find in a telephone directory, in electoral lists or anywhere else. The information is exactly the same although it may be arranged in a slightly different way by the post offices.
The reason, of course, that we do not give forwarding addresses from post offices is that
Supply-Post Office
in many instances this is information not respecting that particular post office but another one far away, and we are not interested in becoming an information service for bill collectors and the like. However, the regular publication of lists of patrons of a particular post office is quite a legitimate process. I appreciated the hon. member's observations on the question of stamp design and the other matters which I will deal with because they were particular points of interest only to him. I will deal with them as soon as we can get the information for him.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka suggested that in some instances people tendered too low for rural mail routes, and suggested there was something rather wrong and improper in this. There is an act of parliament which lays down the obligation. It says "shall" not "may" in so far as the Postmaster General is concerned in requiring him toward the tender to the lowest suitable tenderer. In those circumstances we follow the wishes of parliament. We will be delighted to supply letter carrier service to Parry Sound as soon as they reach the required number of householders.
I was grateful for the observations of the hon. member for Hull, although I am sorry he objects to my visiting post offices. I appreciated the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond and those of the hon. member for Nickel Belt. We will do our best to meet their suggestions.
It was very nice of the hon. member for St. Boniface to say the kind things he did about the new service they are getting in his area. The hon. member for Timmins again spoke on certain questions. There is one particularly that I think I should mention. This is a misunderstanding on his part in so far as observation galleries in post offices are concerned. They are there for one purpose only, and that is the detection of theft by employees in the department. They are specifically not used-our employees are forbidden to use them-for the normal purposes of supervision. They come into operation only when investigation or complaint has disclosed the fact that in a given post office thefts seem to be occurring. At that time investigators who are officially authorized to do it move into those galleries because we have found that post office employees tend not to steal mail when somebody is standing three feet behind them and looking over their shoulders. Therefore our investigators move into those galleries and watch the men from there and this is the only purpose for which they are used.
The hon. member for Edmonton East raised a number of points which we will attempt to deal with, as did the hon. member
49S0

Supply-Post Office
tor Burnaby-Coquitlam, dealing specifically with the minimum number of calls required for letter carrier delivery. This is something which has been changed from time to time by the department and which we are always watching with considerable interest. As the hon. member for Churchill knows, certain matters are now under study in so far as the points he raised are concerned.
The hon. member for Lincoln asked specifically regarding curbside mail boxes. We have had a reasonable degree of success with those in certain communities. In other communities, interestingly enough, they have proved, for whatever reason we do not know, not to have the same popularity. Our general practice is to introduce them into whatever communities would like to have them.
The hon. member for Nipissing raised the question of subpostmasters and that those were now being handled from Ottawa. He implied that he saw political motives in this change, motives which I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, do not exist. The basic problem is simply this. Subpost offices are located in large cities as he knows, or at least in cities, and in many cities there is a tendency, because they do not know anybody in the post office, for the storekeeper or whoever is interested to write to Ottawa. We have decided, rather than overlook some people to centralize all those requests in one place, together with the report from the local people, and then make a decision on that basis. In this way no one is overlooked and it is also possible to take the veterans preference and other matters into consideration.
We are already investigating the matters which the member for Kootenay East raised. With respect to what the hon. member for Timiskaming said, I think I dealt with his remarks by pointing out the people in the gallery who have been with the Post Office Department for 30 or 40 years-I am tremendously proud to be associated with a department of this kind-and who started at the bottom and have ended up at the top. With respect to the question of dissemination of information on promotions, if you have the initiative, Mr. Chairman, you get where you want to go. Promotional opportunities are advertised in every branch of the department.
The hon. member inferred that we were falling behind because we were not sorting mail on the trains as much as we used to and he said that we should go back to this practice. In many cases we would be delighted to go back to it but unfortunately we have been forced off the trains and into the use of trucks because of the elimination of trips, the elimination of trains, the introduction of rail diesel cars which do not have the facilities

and similar reasons. Actually the voluntary doing away with a sortation car on a train in order to go to the road is, to the best of my knowledge, an unheard of thing in the department. It is only when we have to that we do it.
I thank the hon. member for Ottawa East for his very kind words with reference to the Post Office Department. I can tell him that in most cases, interestingly enough, letter carriers are able to carry on until their retirement age. I will probably get hit over the head for saying this but may I say that I do not know of any group of men anywhere in the country who are more genuinely enthusiastic about their job. I think that is what makes them happy when they call on the hon. member and other people. Most of them stay with their jobs until they retire. Those who do not are absorbed internally within the department, almost always as sorters for whom there is a steady demand.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River raised a good number of fairly technical points which I think can perhaps be dealt with directly by correspondence. The hon. member for Vancouver South referred to the question of superannuation. This is very definitely under study at the present time and personally I agree with the point of view he expressed. With respect to the points raised by the hon. member for Sudbury and the question of amalgamation within his area, we are doing our best to work this out to the satisfaction of the citizens of Sudbury. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont referred to imitation stamps. They cannot be confused with regular stamps unless our regulations are broken because on the face of the envelope we only allow our own stamps. These other stamps are quite welcome on the back of envelopes. There is no opportunity for confusion there.
The hon. member for Port Arthur raised a number of technical points. On the question of payment of postage on periodicals I come back to the basic fact that we are in the peculiar position of being next door to a large country which has a large circulation of its publications in our nation. We have to choose between refusing all revenue from them, which happens in some cases, or in other cases allowing them to be mailed in Canada at our rates. It is a nice balance actually to try to determine what the rate picture should be.
So far as the parliamentary frank is concerned, that is entirely a matter for parliament itself to decide. It is written into the statute and it would require an act of parliament to change it. I have sympathy with the hon. member but on the other hand I am very

much aware of the fact that all other people throughout Canada use stamps on their correspondence. Therefore I am inclined to think that members of parliament might want to use stamps on their correspondence when parliament is not sitting.

On that point may I mention this factor? Many people are aware that it is not necessary to put stamps on letters to members of parliament but they are not aware that this privilege lapses within 10 days of the end of a session. Then the member not only has to put up the nickle for the stamp but also has to pay the forfeit. This does not happen rarely but quite often. The minister has a public relations department and perhaps he could do a better job of advertising this situation than individual members of parliament.
I should also like to ask him whether it it is possible for him to procure a breakdown of the figure of $26 million in rough categories as to Canadian and United States periodicals versus newspapers.

There is nothing on file here nor with my officials in the gallery on this point. So far as Canadian publications are concerned, I think it would be difficult, if not impossible, to differentiate between magazines and newspapers. I may be wrong but from memory I think they are bulked together for the purposes of our accounts. However, we certainly could work out some sort of figures to indicate the relationship between publications mailed from the United States and those which are mailed in Canada. I would be glad to develop some figures along those lines.

I appreciate that. I am not asking that the information be given in the house. The minister can send it to me. I imagine that in building up the figure of $26 million some cost factors had to be taken into account. I imagine it is item by item rather than by weight. If the minister could give us some of these factors I should like to have them.

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT OF AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce the appointment of Robert James Rankin, vice-chairman of the national harbours board, to the office of president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority as of August 1. Mr. Rankin will succeed B. J. Roberts, C.B.E., president of the seaway authority since February, 1958, who retires on July 31. Mr. Rankin has been vice-chairman of the national harbours board since February 1, 1958.
In going to his new post Mr. Rankin will add to his already extensive experience in marine matters. He formerly served as chairman of the port of Halifax commission for five years, and was a member of the commission at the time of his appointment as vice-chairman of the national harbours board. He played a notable role prior to that appointment in the economic development of the Atlantic provinces, and was president of the Atlantic provinces economic council in 1957. He is a former newspaperman, joining the staff of the Halifax Herald in 1921 and rising to the post of managing editor of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald before being named vice-president and member of the board of directors. He is a past president of the Canadian Press, serving in that capacity from 1954 to 1956.
Mr. Rankin was born in Chatham, Ontario, a son of the late Mr. and Mrs. J. B. Rankin, and received his education in the schools there. His wife is the former Constance Marguerite Buckler of Annapolis Royal. They have two sons. Mr. Rankin is a veteran of world war I, serving as signals officer with the 1st battalion, C.E.F.
I would also like to refer to the notable contribution Mr. B. J. Roberts has made to Canada over a long period of years. He is a former member and chairman of the national harbours board and a former assistant 79951-0-3124
deputy minister of finance. Over a period of 30 years he served on a number of important boards and commissions, and he was financial adviser to the British commonwealth air training plan during world war II. He was named a commander of the British empire after the war ended.
Mr. Roberts took over as president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority early in 1958, and supervised the final year of construction and the operation of the project since its opening in April last year. His contribution to the present successful operation of the seaway has been a very real one indeed.

1.	Has the government received a copy of the 1959 report of the international commission on radiological protection?
2.	If so, has the government taken any steps to follow the recommendations of this report insofar as lowering the permissible strontium 90 level in food and water is concerned?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteiih (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to part 1 is yes.
The answer to part 2 is as follows. The data contained in the new report of the international commission on radiological protection have been used in the preparation of the annual report of the radiation protection division for 1959. They will continue to form a basis for interpretation of the findings of my department until further recommendations are published by the international commission on radiological protection.
It is to be emphasized, however, that the recommended maximum permissible concentrations given in the new report do not refer to food, but only to air and water. Using additional data contained in the report, members of my department have calculated a maximum permissible level of strontium 90 in the average diet of Canadians. This figure is 79 micromicrocuries strontium 90 per gram of calcium as compared with the ICRP value for water of 33 micromicrocuries strontium 90 per litre. The previous permissible level for strontium 90 in the average Canadian diet based on the 1955 ICRP recommendations was similarly calculated to be 98 micromicrocuries per gram of calcium.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of
Citizenship and Immigration): Mr. Speaker, on Monday the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) inquired concerning the reported eviction of Mr. Kenneth Plain, a member of the Sarnia band, from property held by him on the Sarnia Indian reserve.
Mr. Plain held two parcels of land that were surrendered by the band and sold on terms set by the band in the surrender itself. One parcel comprised 2 acres, the other 9.6 acres. For his interest in these two parcels together Mr. Plain agreed to accept $36,000. The 2 acre parcel has already been paid for in full and title transferred. Mr. Plain received $6,206.90. Total payments made to him amount to $12,612.49. While his valuation of his house located on the 2 acre parcel appears to have been included in the over-all price, he has the right to remove it within six months from the date the purchase price has been paid in full.
Mr. Plain apparently contends that he is not required to move his house until payment has been made in full for both parcels of land. They do not adjoin one another.
The matter has been studied from a legal and equitable standpoint, and it would appear that from neither angle is Mr. Plain on sound ground. Legally the conditions of sale are governed by the surrender itself and the sale contract, not by the option signed by him, which is invalid under section 28 of the Indian Act. The importance of the option is its evidence of his agreement as to price.
Equitably he has already received a substantial payment on account of his house, which was valued in 1957 at $7,000, and may 
move it. The balance owing on the 9.6 acre parcel will be paid to him when the sale of it is completed. If the sale should fall through his ownership of the parcel will be re-established, and he will retain what had been paid thereon.
The purchaser has given Mr. Plain more than the six months' notice required to move his house, and desires possession in order that the land may be used as intended. I may say that the matter is really outside the control of my department, as title has passed.
